title: Book Nine opens: the holy tent as a type of the Church
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK NINE. On the holy tent: that it was a type of the Church in Christ. Love for God and for our brothers has glories plain for all to see, and through both of them the law is brought to its fulfillment (Matthew 22:37–40).
translator_notes: The Greek sentence runs on into section 2, whose first words are its subject ὁ νόμος (‘the law’). To keep the reading natural, ‘the law’ is rendered here in section 1 and section 2 begins with the next sentence. The twin love of God and of the brothers that fulfils the law is cited to the double commandment (Matthew 22:37–40); Romans 13:8–10 is a possible second echo, not cited. σκηνή is rendered ‘tent’, as in Books 1–8 of this work.

title: The heavenly reward, and the Church as the truer tent
english: Cyril: …And whoever has reached this height of renown is illustrious and worthy of admiration, and will be ranked among those who are most truly genuine, as Christ cries out and says, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord’ (Matthew 25:21). For he will enter, and very readily, into the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), and will make his home in the dwelling places above (John 14:2), delighting in good things beyond mind and speech. The prophet Isaiah also says something of this kind: ‘Your eyes will see Jerusalem, rich cities, tents that shall not be shaken; the pegs of the tent shall not be moved, nor shall its cords ever be broken’ (Isaiah 33:20). For the form of this world is passing away, as the Scriptures say (1 Corinthians 7:31), but the hope of what is to come is founded most firmly and is wholly unshakeable. But since all these things are being dissolved, as the Savior’s disciple firmly declared, what sort of people must we be found to be (2 Peter 3:11, 14)? Holy and blameless in his sight (Ephesians 1:4), honoring him as Savior and Redeemer with spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5), and practicing a holy and chosen way of life that agrees with the laws of the Gospel. In just this way the law, of course, sketched in shadow for the people of old this same life, so worthy of reverence and so well worth gaining, when it commanded them to slaughter sheep, to make their offerings by means of blood, to dedicate tithes and firstfruits to God, and thank offerings besides. Yet it laid down that these things must not be done outside the holy tent. And it set apart the tribe of Levi as chosen and dedicated to God (Numbers 3:12), making the thing a type given to us and pointing to ourselves. For we too are called in the divine Scriptures ‘a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession’ (1 Peter 2:9). And we enter the truer tent, which the Lord pitched and not man (Hebrews 8:2), that is, the Church; not appeasing the Maker of all things with calves and goats (Hebrews 9:12), but excelling in a right and blameless faith, and giving off, in a spiritual way, a sweet fragrance through spiritual offerings of fruit. ‘For with such sacrifices God is well pleased’ (Hebrews 13:16), and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth, as the Savior said (John 4:24).

Palladius: You are right. And I would myself say that it befits us to win approval by sacrifices that surpass the law; I will agree to that. But tell me this: was not the old tent set up in the wilderness as a type, for us, of the Church gathered from the nations, showing, though still somewhat dimly, the beauty of the truer tent?

Cyril: Certainly. And I said just a moment ago that the fact that those of Levi’s blood had to be chosen with the greatest care for the sacred ministries would also be, in turn, a type of those who have been called in faith to a holy and blameless life, I mean the life in Christ.
translator_notes: Matthew 25:21 and 25:23 are word for word the same; 25:21 is cited. Isaiah 33:20: Cyril's text has accusative plurals (πόλεις πλουσίας, σκηνάς) where the LXX has πόλις πλουσία, σκηναί, and he omits αὐτῆς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα χρόνον; rendered as Cyril has it. Migne prints ποταμοὺς (‘rivers’), an evident misprint for ποταποὺς (‘of what sort’) from 2 Peter 3:11; Cyril blends 2 Peter 3:11 (ποταποὺς δεῖ) with 3:14 (εὑρεθῆναι, blameless) and Ephesians 1:4 (ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ). The sentence has no finite verb but δεῖ, so it is rendered as the question of 2 Peter 3:11 followed by its answer. ‘Spiritual sacrifices’ is the phrase of 1 Peter 2:5. The rule that offerings must not be made outside the tent is left uncited: it fits Leviticus 17:3–5 (the door of the tent) and the list of offerings fits Deuteronomy 12:6, 13–14, and neither is clearly the one meant. The Levites set apart (Numbers 3:12; also 8:14). ‘Calves and goats’ (Hebrews 9:12) is cited because the next clauses quote Hebrews 8:2 and 13:16. John 4:24: ‘spirit’ is left lower case as in the Gospel verse; the work's title keeps capitals. καρποφορίαι is Cyril's usual word for offerings of fruit; rendered ‘offerings of fruit’.

title: God speaks from heaven; the altar of earth is Emmanuel
english: Palladius: Then would you like us to say a few things about the holy tent and about the priesthood under the law, letting our discussion examine closely what was reverently decreed about both?

Cyril: It is no easy matter. It will take, I think, long labor and sweat on our part, Palladius, both to be able to understand these things and to explain them as well. Still, if you agree, let us go through them trusting in God; for you have learned that he says plainly, ‘Who gave a mouth to man? And who made the hard of hearing and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God? And now go, and I will open your mouth’ (Exodus 4:11–12).
Palladius: Go on, then, and make the Giver of wisdom your helper in this as well.

Cyril: Then I will go on, and I will speak, having gathered with care what the sacred Scriptures say. God, the Maker of all things, came down in the form of fire upon Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18), and laid down laws by which each thing that was to be done might be brought to what is upright and genuine. Then, drawing them away from their former error and setting them as far as possible from the false worship of Egypt, he spoke to Moses, who was then acting as mediator. ‘Thus you shall say,’ he says, ‘to the house of Jacob, and declare to the sons of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver for yourselves, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves’ (Exodus 20:22–23). He did not allow them to serve gods falsely so called. Instead he commands that they must hold fast to him alone who came from above and from heaven, who by his very being holds power over all things, and whose glory lies not in the fine colors of material things but in showing that heaven is his own. But it was in some way necessary that those who had been commanded to depart from their ancient impiety and profane worship should pass at once to another custom, and come, as it were, under a yoke: the worship of him who is God by nature. For a mind left slack is unrestrained and all too ready to be carried off into anything whatever, even the most outlandish; but when fear and anxious care hang over it, it darts quite readily toward what is right and inclines toward what is profitable. And since we come to the Father through the Son, for ‘no one comes to the Father,’ he says, ‘except through me’ (John 14:6), he therefore, as was necessary, laid down in law the types of our approach through the Son and of the offering made in him, saying: ‘You shall make me an altar of earth, and on it you shall sacrifice your whole burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your sheep and your oxen, in every place where I cause my name to be named; and I will come to you and bless you. And if you make me an altar of stones, you shall not build them of hewn stones; for you have put your chisel to it, and it is defiled’ (Exodus 20:24–25). By the altar of earth he means Emmanuel, ‘for the Word became flesh’ (John 1:14); and the nature of the flesh is earth from earth.
translator_notes: Exodus 4:11–12: Cyril's text adds Κύριος (‘the Lord God’) where the LXX has οὐκ ἐγὼ ὁ θεός; rendered as he has it. Exodus 20:22–23: the opening ‘Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and declare to the sons of Israel’ belongs to LXX Exodus 20:22 (the Hebrew has only ‘Thus you shall say to the sons of Israel’); it also matches Exodus 19:3. Migne prints Ὑμεῖςἑωράκατε run together (OCR join), read as Ὑμεῖς ἑωράκατε. ‘Him who came from above and from heaven … over all’ may echo John 3:31 (ὁ ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος … ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἐρχόμενος ἐπάνω πάντων), but here Cyril applies it to God speaking from heaven at Sinai; left uncited. The sentence on the loosened mind has no contrasting particle: δειμάτων τε καὶ φροντίδος ἐπηρτημένων is read as a genitive absolute (‘when fear and care hang over it’), so ‘but’ is supplied from the sense, which carries the argument that the people needed a yoke. ἐγχειρίδιον (a hand blade) is rendered ‘chisel’. The last Greek sentence ends with φύσις, the first word of section 4; it is rendered here so that the clause reads whole, and section 4 begins with the next sentence.

title: The uncut stones, and the first gifts for the sanctuary
english: Cyril: …In Christ, then, lies all our offering of fruit and every approach; for he himself says, ‘Apart from me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5). For just as through him we have obtained access (Romans 5:2), so too through him every sacrifice of those who have received the faith is acceptable. And to those who set up the altar of earth he promises his coming and a blessing: ‘For I will come to you,’ he says, ‘and bless you’ (Exodus 20:24). For when we had received through the all-wise Moses the types of the truth, the truth itself also shone forth in its due season, that is, Christ, through whom and in whom we have been enriched with the blessing that comes from above and from the Father (Ephesians 1:3), sealed for adoption as sons in the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). And this too, again, is fulfilled in Christ: ‘And if you make me an altar of stones,’ he says, ‘you shall not build them of hewn stones’ (Exodus 20:25). He does not allow the stones dedicated to God to be wounded with iron. For Christ was the chosen stone, the precious cornerstone (Isaiah 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6): unwounded by sins, and knowing nothing of suffering the blows that come from the devil; not divided between God and the world, even though he became flesh, but holy through and through; not divided into God separately and man separately after the ineffable union, that is, his coming together with flesh, but being one and the same, God and also man. For he is in no way divided, as the wise Paul also writes (1 Corinthians 1:13).
Palladius: So the altar of earth, and the uncut stones as well, signify Christ, in the ways already described?

Cyril: So I say; for the law is spiritual, as the Scriptures say (Romans 7:14). And once he had outlined in riddles the mystery of Christ and our approach through him, then, at that very point, God planned to show beforehand the form of the Church as well. So he called Moses, and Joshua with him, up onto Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:12–13). And understand from this that even to the holy prophets themselves the Father is approachable through the Son; for Moses and Joshua go up together. For it is written: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and take firstfruits for me from all whose heart moves them; you shall take my firstfruits. And these are the firstfruits that you shall take from them: gold and silver, bronze and blue, purple and double scarlet, and twisted fine linen, and goats’ hair, and rams’ skins dyed red, and skins dyed blue, and wood that does not decay, and sardius stones, and stones for engraving, for the ephod and for the robe that reaches to the feet. And you shall make me a sanctuary, and I will be seen among you. And you shall make it for me according to all that I show you on the mountain, the pattern of the tent and the pattern of all its furnishings; so you shall make it’ (Exodus 25:1–9). Do you see how he urges the peoples to bring as offering what is profitable and most needful for the building up of the Church, bringing gladly what matches their means and their will? For he did not ask only for gold…
translator_notes: Section 4 opens with φύσις, the last word of the sentence begun in section 3; it is rendered there. προσαγωγή carries both ‘offering’ and ‘access’; Cyril plays on both, so the first use is rendered ‘approach’ and the second ‘access’ (δι’ οὗ καὶ τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐσχήκαμεν is the wording of Romans 5:2; Ephesians 2:18 is close). ‘Every sacrifice … acceptable through him’ may echo 1 Peter 2:5; left uncited. The pairing of Moses with types and Christ with truth recalls John 1:17, but Cyril does not quote it; left uncited. Ephesians 1:3 (blessing in Christ) and 1:13 (sealed with the Holy Spirit, with adoption from 1:5) are cited as clear allusions. Iron tools on altar stones echoes Deuteronomy 27:5; left uncited, since Cyril is explaining Exodus 20:25. Isaiah 28:16 LXX gives the adjectives in Cyril's order (ἐκλεκτὸν ἀκρογωνιαῖον ἔντιμον); 1 Peter 2:6 quotes it. 1 Corinthians 1:13 is Paul's question ‘Is Christ divided?’, which Cyril turns into a statement. Ἰησοῦς here is Joshua son of Nun, rendered ‘Joshua’ as in Books 2–8; Cyril's point that the Father is reached ‘through the Son’ rests on the fact that Joshua bears the name Jesus in Greek, which English cannot show without adding words. Exodus 24:12–13: God calls Moses up the mountain (24:12) and he goes up with Joshua (24:13). Exodus 25:1–9 follows the LXX (sardius stones, ‘I will be seen among you’, ξύλα ἄσηπτα, ‘wood that does not decay’, kept because Cyril later reads it of Christ's incorrupt body). The section ends mid-sentence; section 5 continues it.

title: Small gifts accepted; God seen in the Church; the ark
english: Cyril: …or for things that many people perhaps find hard to come by, but also goats’ hair and rams’ skins, showing that even what is small and cheap, if the one who has chosen to bring an offering has nothing finer, is not rejected by God; perhaps it even ranks equal with the most precious gifts, or wins greater praise. So too Christ, of course, did not leave without admiration the widow in Jerusalem who brought to the treasury something small and very easy to come by (Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4), yet perhaps great for those in the deepest poverty, for whom even parting with the cheapest things is likely to be a hardship. When the firstfruits had been received, ‘You shall make me a sanctuary,’ he says, ‘and I will be seen among you’ (Exodus 25:8). For Christ appears in the Church and shines upon those within it, as the Psalms say: ‘God is the Lord, and he has shone forth upon us’ (Psalm 118:27). And observe how, although he had come down on the mountain in the form of fire and had been seen by all the people (Exodus 19:11, 18), as it is written, he says, as though he had not yet appeared, ‘I will be seen among you,’ once the sanctuary has been raised. He all but cries aloud, as one can clearly see, that those visions were shadows of the true sight of God, and that the true revelation is Christ, in whom we have seen the Father himself (John 14:9). Indeed, when the Jews supposed that on Mount Sinai they had truly seen the God of all things, he showed them how utterly foolish their thinking was, saying: ‘You have not heard his voice, nor seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe the one whom he sent’ (John 5:37–38). So he says, ‘I will be seen among you,’ when the sanctuary has been raised. And this was a type of the Church, which came into being in the likeness of the Church above. For he says, ‘You shall make it for me according to all that I show you on the mountain; so you shall make it’ (Exodus 25:9). For there was shown to the blessed Moses, as I said, a type of the holy churches, and also he himself who became man for our sake, shaped in many forms as though in shadow. Yet on each of the patterns the discussion would grow long and drawn out, and full of minute detail. But since some things belong to and suit the construction of the objects that were made, while others look toward the purpose of spiritual contemplation, come, let us speak of what is useful for this purpose, and let the rest go.
Palladius: I do not understand what you mean.

Cyril: Then look at what I mean, for you will understand it, I think, quite without effort. He commanded that an ark be made of wood that does not decay, overlaid inside and out with pure gold, and bearing within it what are called the testimonies, that is, the law on tablets. And the instructions about it did not stop there: he commands, further, that poles be made of wood that does not decay, gilded in the same way, and gold rings, and a twisted border all around. He fixed the length, breadth and height of the work (Exodus 25:10–16). But if someone wished to probe such things very closely in the mystical sense, he will perhaps find out what the ark is, and the…
translator_notes: Psalm 118:27 is LXX Psalm 117:27 (θεὸς κύριος καὶ ἐπέφανεν ἡμῖν); ἐπέφανεν is rendered ‘has shone forth’ to keep both ‘appeared’ and ‘shone’, which Cyril's own verbs (ἐπιφαίνεται, ἐπιλάμπει) draw on. ‘Seen by all the people’ at Sinai: Exodus 19:11 (the Lord comes down ‘before all the people’) with 19:18 (the fire). John 14:9 for ‘in whom we have seen the Father’ is a clear allusion. The subject of διήλεγχε (‘he showed them … foolish’) is Christ, who speaks John 5:37–38. The Church ‘in the likeness of the one above’ may recall Galatians 4:26 or Hebrews 12:22–23; left uncited. Exodus 25:9 (also 25:40) for the pattern on the mountain. ἰσχνομυθία (‘thin talk’) is rendered ‘minute detail’. ὠδίνουσαν (‘in labour with’) is rendered ‘bearing within it’ to keep the image of birth without a heavier phrase. στρεπτὰ κύκλῳ follows LXX Exodus 25:11 (κυμάτια στρεπτὰ χρυσᾶ κύκλῳ), rendered ‘a twisted border all around’. The ark details gather Exodus 25:10–16 (ark, gold, rings, poles, the testimony put inside). The section ends mid-sentence; the next word, μαρτύρια (‘testimonies’), opens section 6. John 5:37: the Gospel has πώποτε (‘ever’), which Cyril's text omits; rendered ‘You have not heard’ as he quotes it.

title: The ark as a type of Christ; its gold as his Godhead
english: Cyril: …the testimonies, and what need there was for wood that does not rot. But if he should perhaps pry closely into what the gold on the ark is meant to show, and into the things put together for the time being for use and ornament, I mean the mouldings, the twisted work, the rings and the carrying poles (Exodus 25:11–14), he will find the matter hard. Unable to fit a mystical sense to them, he will probably say more than is needed and pile a mass of idle words on the ears of those keener to learn. And what I say holds true, perhaps, not of the ark alone; I would add that it holds also of the other things he commanded to be made.

Palladius: Your thinking and your words seem to me not unconvincing. So set aside what concerns, as you say, proportion and use, that is, the ornament of the finished works, and hurry straight to what our contemplation needs: explain without hesitation in what way Christ himself is signified to us by the things shown as a pattern, that is, the things that were built.

Cyril: Well then, I will try, as far as one can speak and understand. But if I miss the truth, and reach less than I ought toward the height of these thoughts, be forgiving. For seeing in a mirror and in a riddle (1 Corinthians 13:12) can at times trip up even a precise and sensible mind.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: The ark, Palladius, would be for us a type and image of Christ. For when we look closely at the manner in which the Only-begotten became man, we shall see the Word who is from God the Father dwelling, as in an ark, in the temple that is from the Virgin. For ‘all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt in him bodily’ (Colossians 2:9), as the Scriptures say. And the testimonies in the ark were the Word of God. Its wood did not rot, and it was adorned inside and out with pure and thoroughly tested gold (Exodus 25:10–11). For the body of Christ is incorruptible: it is held fast in incorruption, as by a kind of gold, by the power and radiance of the Word who dwells in it, and by the nature and life-giving working of the Holy Spirit. That is why Christ is also said to give life. For the Word who is from God the Father, being Life by nature, himself brought his own temple back to life by the power of his own Spirit, setting it above corruption. For ‘his flesh knows no corruption,’ in the words of holy Paul (Acts 13:37; Acts 2:31). And he also told the Jews somewhere, speaking of his own body, ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up’ (John 2:19); and Peter, too, says that he was put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit (1 Peter 3:18). So the gold is a symbol of the surpassingly bright Godhead, laid over the holy body, as it were, and instilling in it, beyond telling, his own brightness and incorruption, in a way known only to the divine nature itself, which is beyond understanding. For if ‘the righteous in due…
translator_notes: Ends mid-quotation of Matthew 13:43 ('Οἱ δίκαιοι κατὰ | καιροὺς'); the citation stands in s7 where the quotation closes. τέως ('for the time being') rendered as such: the fittings served the tabernacle's use and ornament, not a mystical sense. Source has a stray period in 'συμμετρίαν. τε' (OCR); read as συμμετρίαν τε. παραδεδειγμένα echoes the 'pattern shown' of Exodus 25:9, 40 but is vocabulary, not a quotation: uncited. Λόγος δὲ ἦν Θεοῦ: Migne capitalises; the double sense (the tablets as God's word, and the Word within the temple of the body) is intended, so 'the Word of God' is kept with capital W. 'his own Spirit' (τοῦ ἰδίου πνεύματος, lower case in Migne): capitalised because Cyril has just named the Holy Spirit and regularly calls the Spirit the Son's own. Colossians 2:9: Cyril has aorist κατῴκησε ('dwelt') for NT present κατοικεῖ. 'His flesh knows no corruption': Cyril credits Paul, so Acts 13:37 (Paul at Pisidian Antioch, 'did not see corruption') is cited first; the wording ἡ σὰρξ αὐτοῦ matches Peter at Acts 2:31, so both are cited inline (both quote Psalm 16:10, LXX 15:10); οἶδε may be itacism for εἶδε ('saw'). 'περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος' echoes John 2:21 (part of the John 2:19 context, not separately cited). 1 Peter 3:18 πνεύματι rendered 'in the Spirit', which keeps Cyril's instrumental reading open without forcing it. 'τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτοῦ λαμπρότητα': αὐτοῦ (masc./neut.) cannot refer to θεότης (fem.); taken as the Word's own brightness, hence 'his own'. 'Life by nature' may echo John 11:25 / 14:6 but no clear quotation: uncited. 'Christ is said to give life' may recall John 5:21; doubtful, uncited.

title: The golden poles and rings; Christ the mercy seat
english: Cyril: …time will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father’ (Matthew 13:43), what then will the glory of Christ himself be? And how can his radiance not pass beyond all thought and speech? The poles that carry the ark are gold, the rings are gold too, and so is everything on it; for those around him share in his glory, since they are, as it were, fastened to him in love and sanctification, and are of use. Such, too, were the blessed disciples, who received from him the power that befits God, grew rich, by participation, in the brightness of the supreme excellence that comes from above, and for this reason worked divine signs.
Palladius: You are right.

Cyril: ‘And besides the ark,’ he says, ‘you shall make a mercy seat, a cover of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and one and a half cubits wide. And you shall make two cherubim of wrought gold, and set them at the two ends of the mercy seat. One cherub shall be made at this end, and one cherub at the other end of the mercy seat; and you shall make the two cherubim at the two ends. The cherubim shall spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, and their faces shall be toward one another; the faces of the cherubim shall be toward the mercy seat. And you shall set the mercy seat on the top, above, and into the ark you shall put the testimonies that I will give you. And I will make myself known to you from there, and I will speak to you from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, about everything that I command you for the sons of Israel’ (Exodus 25:17–22).
Palladius: Then what do you say the mercy seat is?

Cyril: As far as the letter and the shadow go, it was made of pure gold, and was in some way fitted on, lying upon the ark; that is why it is called a cover. And those adorned with the honors of the priesthood, when they turned toward it and looked at it, were held to be turning toward God and looking at him. But we say that the mercy seat, if it is understood spiritually, is he who became man for our sake, ‘whom God put forward as a mercy seat through faith, in his blood, to show his righteousness’ (Romans 3:25). For so Paul says. And John, the wisest disciple, also writes to us: ‘Little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world’ (1 John 2:1–2). For through him come propitiation, every prayer, and the asking of good things. For ‘until now,’ he says, ‘you have asked nothing in my name (John 16:24); ask, and it will be given to you’ (Matthew 7:7). So he himself is the mercy seat. For through him the Father is gracious to us; in him every prayer reaches its end; and through him we draw near, since in no other way are we acceptable. That is why he says, ‘I am the way’ (John 14:6); and, ‘I am the door’ (John 10:9); and, ‘No one comes to the…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation of Matthew 13:43 begun at the end of s6. Cyril's text has κατὰ καιρούς ('in due time'), which is not in Matthew 13:43; rendered as he quotes it. Ends mid-quotation of John 14:6 ('Οὐδεὶς ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸν | Πατέρα'); s8 carries the citation where the quotation closes, and 'I am the way' here is already cited to John 14:6. Exodus 25:17–22: LXX and English verse numbers agree here. Variants in Cyril's text against Rahlfs LXX: χρυσᾶ τορνευτά ('of wrought/turned gold') for χρυσοτορευτά; ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ἄνωθεν ('on the top, above') for ἐπὶ τὴν κιβωτὸν ἄνωθεν. Translated as Cyril has them. ἱλαστήριον is rendered 'mercy seat' throughout, including in Romans 3:25 (often 'propitiation' or 'sacrifice of atonement'), because Cyril's argument rests on Paul using the same word as Exodus; ἱλασμός (1 John 2:2) is 'propitiation' and ἵλεως 'gracious' to keep the word family visible. ἐπικειμένη is feminine though ἱλαστήριον is neuter (Migne as printed); sense unaffected. 'He who became man for our sake' (τὸν δι' ἡμᾶς γενόμενον ἄνθρωπον): kept as 'became man', not 'the man who came to be', which would misstate Cyril's Christology. 'Ask, and it will be given to you': Cyril joins John 16:24 to the wording of Matthew 7:7 (identical in Luke 11:9); John 16:24 itself ends 'and you will receive'. 'I am the door': John 10:9 (also 10:7). 'Through him we draw near' may echo Ephesians 2:18 / Hebrews 7:25; doubtful, uncited. The disciples' divine signs may recall Luke 9:1 or Acts 1:8; doubtful, uncited. ἁγιασμός rendered 'sanctification' (not 'holiness'); ὑπεροχή 'supreme excellence'.

title: Angels around the mercy seat; God's face and ways beyond sight
english: Cyril: …Father except through me’ (John 14:6). Yet even though the only-begotten Word of God became like us, lowering himself into humanity and self-emptying (Philippians 2:7), it still belongs to him by nature to be thought of in the glory that befits God and to exist in the heights that are above creation, just as he did, of course, before the flesh. That is why the cherubim stand around the mercy seat, covering it with their wings, turned toward it and always keeping their faces fixed on it (Exodus 25:20); and their station on the right and on the left is a clear proof that they are its guard of honor. And the fact that the cherubim always look toward the mercy seat seems to hint at how intent, and, as it were, insatiable, the highest powers are in beholding God.

The prophet Isaiah, too, portrays the Son in the form proper to him, saying, ‘I saw the Lord of hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and seraphim stood around him’ (Isaiah 6:1–2); and he says that six wings had grown on each, and that with two they covered the feet, with two the faces, and with the others they flew (Isaiah 6:2). If someone thinks that the seraphim were covering the face of God, and his feet too, there is nothing unreasonable in taking it so. For if we put the meaning of the word ‘seraphim’ into Greek, we shall find that it signifies a fullness of knowledge, or an outpouring of wisdom. By their posture, then, these all-wise and highest powers hint very clearly that it is not lawful for God’s face to be seen by anyone. For the nature that is beyond all understanding is wholly beyond sight, and ‘dwells in unapproachable light’ (1 Timothy 6:16), in the words of blessed Paul; and ‘no one shall see the face of God and live’ (Exodus 33:20), as God rightly told the most holy Moses. Nor could anyone know his footsteps and his ways. For it is written, ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!’ (Romans 11:33) Blessed David, too, sings and strikes up a wise song: ‘Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps will not be known’ (Psalm 77:19). For just as no one could see a track in water, whether of a man, perhaps, or of a ship, or of the creatures that swim in it, so no one could make out the divine and ineffable ways. The feet would be a type of these ways.

But if someone should suppose that the holy seraphim cover their own faces and feet with their wings, let us understand that it is not lawful to see the beginning or the end of the wisdom, or knowledge, that concerns God. For it too is beyond grasp, and beyond the human mind. The beginning of every body is the head, and its end the feet. So the mercy seat is Christ, who, even when he appeared in the flesh, is no less God and Lord, by nature and in truth, and has even the highest powers standing around him in a circle as servants. And the sacred word also tells us somewhere that after Satan withdrew, giving up his testing of Christ when he had fasted for us, angels came and served him (Matthew 4:11). For ‘they are ministering spirits…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation of John 14:6 begun at the end of s7. It ends mid-word inside Hebrews 1:14 ('Πνεύματα γάρ εἰσι λει | τουργικά'): the English stops at 'For ‘they are ministering spirits' and the quotation closes in s9, which must carry the inline citation (Hebrews 1:14); it is not cited here so that no citation sits inside an open quotation. Psalm 77:19 = LXX Psalm 76:20 (Hebrew 77:20). Isaiah 6:1: Cyril's 'Κύριον Σαβαώθ' adds Sabaoth (from 6:3, 6:5) to LXX 6:1; rendered 'the Lord of hosts'. Isaiah 6:2 LXX lacks a possessive with 'the face' and 'the feet', which is why Cyril can weigh whether the seraphim cover God's face and feet or their own; the English keeps 'the feet', 'the faces' without a possessive for that reason. Cyril gives the feet first, then the faces; order kept. The etymology 'fullness of knowledge' is the one Philo and later writers give for 'cherubim'; Cyril applies it, with 'outpouring of wisdom', to 'seraphim'. Translated as he has it, without correction. ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ σχήματι taken as 'in the form proper to him' (the Son in his own divine glory, matching the preceding point), not 'in the same posture'. 'As God rightly told the most holy Moses' replaces the pronoun παρ' αὐτοῦ with 'God' so readers do not take it as Paul; no concept added. ἄποπτος rendered 'beyond sight'. κένωσις: clear allusion to Philippians 2:7 ('emptied himself'), cited. Exodus 25:20 cited for the cherubim facing and covering the mercy seat (Cyril's paraphrase of the passage quoted in s7). The untraceable ship's track may recall Wisdom 5:10 or Proverbs 30:19; doubtful, uncited. 'Appeared in the flesh' (ἐν σαρκὶ πεφηνώς) may echo 1 Timothy 3:16 (ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί), but the verb differs; uncited. 'Beyond all understanding' may echo Philippians 4:7; uncited.

title: Christ above the mercy seat; the golden table and the bread from heaven
english: Cyril: …ministering, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation’ (Hebrews 1:14). ‘From above the mercy seat I will make myself known to you,’ he says, ‘and I will speak with you’ (Exodus 25:22). Through this too, I think, he shows two things. The first is that Christ, though he is man, will speak things beyond human nature, and will not keep only within the limits of his self-emptying (Philippians 2:7), because by nature he is God and from God. For he said, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), and, ‘He who has seen me has seen the Father’ (John 14:9). Or perhaps it is this: He is known above the mercy seat and the cherubim, that is, in a preeminence and glory beyond what is human and beyond every created thing, the highest and most exalted of which are the seraphim, even though he became flesh (John 1:14). The mercy seat was of gold, and so were the seraphim themselves (Exodus 25:17–18). For God is the glorious and most beautiful nature, while created things bear a likeness to him by participation. To those who stand around him and near him he imparts a share in his own natural radiance, as light, reflected onto something near it, lights up whatever it meets with its own brightness.
Palladius: That is right, and the argument has been finely worked out for us in keeping with the truth.

Cyril: After the making of the mercy seat, he sketches the mystery of Christ for us in yet another way, saying, ‘And you shall make a table of pure gold’ (Exodus 25:23). He commanded that rings be fixed to it and golden carrying poles be put through them, and he set out very clearly its measurements and the methods of fine workmanship by which it would attain the highest beauty of form (Exodus 25:24–28). ‘And you shall set on the table,’ he says, ‘the loaves of the presence, before me continually’ (Exodus 25:30). He also ordered that its vessels be made of gold: dishes and incense cups, and ladles too, and pitchers for drink offerings (Exodus 25:29). Was not the bread from heaven plainly being shown to us here, the bread that would be set out at the appointed times on the holy tables of the churches and that gives life to the world (John 6:33)?
Palladius: Very plainly.

Cyril: And the dishes and incense cups, the ladles and pitchers, and all the things by which the mystical and most sacred service of the holy table is carried out: would they not be a type of the sacred treasures, my friend?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: But these things are in Exodus. Concerning the table, and the setting out of the loaves as well, the lawgiver has spoken his oracles in Leviticus. There he widens the command, as it were, and teaches clearly how the loaves are to be set out, speaking thus (Leviticus 24:5–9): ‘And you shall take fine flour and make twelve loaves of it; each loaf shall contain two tenths. And you shall set them in two rows, six loaves to a row, on the pure table before the Lord. And you shall put pure frankincense and salt on the row, and they shall be for the loaves as a memorial, set before the Lord. On the Sabbath day…
translator_notes: Opens mid-word in Hebrews 1:14 (λει|τουργικά) continued from §8; ends mid-quotation of Leviticus 24:8, continued in §10. Exodus 25:22 is paraphrased (LXX order: γνωσθήσομαί σοι ἐκεῖθεν καὶ λαλήσω σοι ἄνωθεν τοῦ ἱλαστηρίου). Cyril writes 'Seraphim' where Exodus has cherubim, following his §8 identification of the mercy-seat figures with the Seraphim of Isaiah 6; kept as written. 'Exodus 25:17–18' marks his reference to the gold mercy seat and gold figures; 'Exodus 25:24–28' marks his summary of rings, poles, measures and workmanship (LXX numbering matches English in Exodus 25). 'Philippians 2:7' is cited for κένωσις (self-emptying), a clear term allusion. The subject of σκιαγραφεῖ / ἐπιτάξας / προστέταχεν is the One giving the command to Moses and is capitalised; ὁ νομοθέτης ('the lawgiver') may mean God or Moses, so it and its pronouns are left lowercase. κειμήλια = treasured stored valuables; probably the church's liturgical vessels; rendered 'sacred treasures' without adding 'of the churches'. ἀπεξεσμένος (polished, smoothed) rendered 'finely worked out'; the Greek is passive with ἡμῖν ('for us'), so no 'you' is supplied. Leviticus 24:7 LXX 'εἰς ἄρτους' rendered 'for the loaves'.

title: The loaves of the presence, the firstfruits of dough, and the golden lampstand
english: Cyril: …it shall be set before the Lord continually, before the sons of Israel, as an everlasting covenant. And it shall belong to Aaron and to his sons, and they shall eat them in a holy place; for this is most holy for them, from the offerings made to the Lord, a perpetual ordinance’ (Leviticus 24:8–9). In Numbers, again, he showed us the bread that is from heaven and also from us as one bread, for the Word, though God by nature, became like us and dwelt among us (John 1:14). He showed this when he said to Moses, the revealer of sacred rites: ‘Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you go into the land into which I am bringing you, then, when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall take off a portion set apart for the Lord, the firstfruits of your dough. You shall set apart a loaf as an offering; as an offering is taken from the threshing floor, so you shall take off the firstfruits of your dough, and you shall give an offering to the Lord throughout your generations’ (Numbers 15:18–21). Through these words one could see the mystery of the truth without effort. It will be discussed by us in detail and with precision at its proper time, when our discourse has passed on to another labor of writing. For the present, though, Palladius, there is one thing, I think, that anyone would marvel at.
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: That in setting Emmanuel before our eyes in many forms, he portrays him once more through yet another passage. For he says to Moses: ‘And you shall make a lampstand of pure gold; you shall make the lampstand finely wrought. Its shaft and its branches, its cups, its knobs and its lilies shall be of one piece with it. Six branches from the second side’ (Exodus 25:31–32). Then, after adding the parts that serve the work’s beauty and use, I mean the lilies, the knobs and the almond ornaments (Exodus 25:33–35), he declared again: ‘All of it finely wrought, from one piece of pure gold. And you shall make its seven lamps, and you shall set up its lamps, and they shall shine from the one front. And its oil vessel and its trays you shall make of pure gold; you shall make all these vessels from a talent of pure gold. See that you make them according to the pattern shown you on the mountain’ (Exodus 25:36–40). So the lampstand, which stands as a type of Christ, is of gold. For the Son is God by nature and in truth, and the divine splendor and preeminence must be likened to gold, as we also laid down earlier. It is finely wrought because Emmanuel is beautiful beyond all words in the beauty of form that the mind perceives. For it is written, ‘Fairer in beauty than the sons of men’ (Psalm 45:2). So the finely wrought shape of the lampstand would show Emmanuel’s surpassing beauty of form very well, and plainly this is the beauty that befits God. He says that branches grow out to the right and to the left, as from a tree, and spring up together with the central shaft, rising to an equal height (Exodus 25:32). For the Only-begotten, though he is one by nature and, as God, simple in essence, seems to be many in his various activities; yet there is nothing brought in or foreign…
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation of Leviticus 24:8–9 (the whole quotation is cited as Leviticus 24:5–9 at its start in §9); ends mid-sentence, continued in §11. Cyril's text reads προσθήσεται where LXX Leviticus 24:8 has προθήσεται; rendered 'set before' in either case. Psalm 44:3 LXX = Psalm 45:2 English. Numbers 15:18–21 follows LXX with minor variation (πορεύεσθαι for εἰσπορεύεσθαι). Exodus 25:31–32 is abridged by Cyril ('Six branches from the second side'); rendered as written, not filled out. LXX has τορευτή (worked in relief); Cyril reads τορνευτή (turned), which he takes as 'beautifully shaped': rendered 'finely wrought' throughout so his argument reads. καρυίσκοι (LXX 'nutlets', almond-shaped ornaments) rendered 'almond ornaments'. ἐπαρυστήρ (oil-pourer / lamp filler) rendered 'oil vessel'. ἱεροφάντης rendered 'revealer of sacred rites'. The 'other labor of writing' where Cyril promises to treat Numbers 15 is not named; possibly the Glaphyra on Numbers or a later book of this work (uncertain, no reference given). John 1:14 cited for γέγονε ... καθ' ἡμᾶς ... καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν. 'Exodus 25:32' marks Cyril's paraphrase of the branches; 'rising to an equal height' is his description, not the verse's wording.

title: The lampstand all of gold; seven lamps shining toward the front
english: Cyril: …in him, even if in the dignities that befit God he may somehow be thought of as not simple. For he is understood as light and life, and power and incorruption. It was because he wished to teach that nothing in him is acquired from outside, I think, that he added, ‘Let the knobs and the branches be of one piece with it; all of it finely wrought of pure gold’ (Exodus 25:36). That is, he is wholly and entirely God. He was not made holy in the way created things are, nor is he like, say, the angels, who are understood to exist in a nature of their own but are made splendid by his grace and glory, and are overlaid with the gift of the Spirit as if with pure gold. Rather, he is by nature the very thing itself: God, the purest and highest nature. There are seven lamps, because the enlightening that comes from Christ takes many forms: ‘To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,’ and ‘the discerning of spirits,’ and the rest (1 Corinthians 12:8–10). The number seven, again, is a sign of perfection. Emmanuel is wholly perfect, both in his own nature, as God, and in the distribution of his gifts, for he is present in full in those worthy to receive them. For, in John’s words, ‘He does not give the Spirit by measure’ (John 3:34), but ‘from the fullness we have all received’ (John 1:16). Then he says, ‘And you shall set up the lamps, and they shall shine from the one front’ (Exodus 25:37). What this placing might be, he showed clearly in Numbers, saying: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and say to him: When you set up the lamps on one side, facing the front of the lampstand, the seven lamps shall give light. And Aaron did so: on the one side, facing the front of the lampstand, he lit its lamps, as the Lord had commanded Moses’ (Numbers 8:1–3). Notice, then, that the seven lamps, turned to face the front of the lampstand, sent their light to those who looked on. For the divine and spiritual light does not shine on those who stand behind and lie, as it were, under God’s turning away, but on those who have been brought into his sight through sanctification and now stand face to face with him through boldness in faith and the noble dignity of an upright life. For everything that dwells in wickedness and disobedience is loathsome and hateful, but what is obedient and willing to be guided is precious and under God’s care. For to the Jews, who chose to abuse him without restraint, he also says through the voice of Isaiah, ‘When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you’ (Isaiah 1:15). But ‘the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous’ (Psalm 34:15), as is sung in the Psalms.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: The inspired Zechariah also clearly mentions this holy lampstand, for he said (Zechariah 4:1–3): ‘And the angel who was speaking with me returned and woke me, as a man is woken from his sleep, and he said to me, “What do you see?” And I said, “I have looked, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, and its bowl, and seven lamps on it, and two olive trees above it, one on the right of its bowl, and one…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence continued from §10 (οὐδὲν εἰσκεκριμένον ἢ ὀθνεῖον | ἐν αὐτῷ); ends mid-quotation of Zechariah 4:3, continued in §12. 'Light and life, and power and incorruption' may echo John 1:4, John 8:12 and 1 Corinthians 1:24, but the allusion is not clear enough to cite. κατακεχρισμένοι (from καταχρίω) can mean 'anointed' or 'smeared over'; with 'as if with pure gold' it reads as gold overlay (angels plated, Christ solid gold), so rendered 'overlaid'. τελείως ἔγκειται τοῖς ἑλεῖν ἀξίοις is compressed (ἔγκειμαι: press upon, be devoted to, be present in); rendered 'He is present in full in those worthy to receive them', keeping Emmanuel as the subject of ἔγκειται; sense supported by the John quotations that follow; still a compressed phrase. 1 Corinthians 12:8–10 is quoted loosely (word of wisdom, word of knowledge, then discerning of spirits from v. 10). John 3:34 and John 1:16 are both attributed to 'John' (the Baptist's words in the Gospel); Cyril's text of John 1:16 lacks αὐτοῦ, so rendered 'from the fullness'. ἐν ἀποστροφῇ τῇ παρὰ Θεῷ taken as lying under God's turning away, matching the Isaiah 1:15 quotation that follows. Psalm 33:16 LXX = Psalm 34:15 English. Zechariah 4:2 LXX: Cyril omits the seven oil pourers (ἑπτὰ ἐπαρυστρίδες) and reads 'its bowl' for 'the bowl above it'; rendered as he quotes. ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοί (LXX 'speaking in me') rendered 'speaking with me'; Cyril does not build on the 'in' here. θεσπέσιος rendered 'inspired'. Ἰουδαίοις kept as 'the Jews' as Cyril wrote.

title: The seven eyes of the Lord and the two olive branches
english: Cyril: …and one on the left.” And I asked and said to the angel who spoke in me, “My lord, what are these?” And he said to me, “Do you not know what these are?” And I said, “No, my lord.”’ (Zechariah 4:3–5) So the blessed prophet asked, ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the divine angel, after inserting a short account (Zechariah 4:6–10), interprets the vision and refers the making of the lampstand to Christ, saying of the seven lamps on it, ‘These are the eyes of the Lord, which look upon the whole earth.’ (Zechariah 4:10) For if we must say something in rather bodily terms, the Godhead sees us with countless eyes and surveys human affairs, ‘knowing what is in the darkness,’ as it is written, ‘and the light is with him’ (Daniel 2:22). For if God puts light even into us who are in the world, he would surely be rich in it himself, since he has it in his own nature before all others. Or if some suspect that this is not so, it is perhaps time to cry out to those who have chosen to think that way: ‘Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, be wise at last. He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive?’ (Psalm 94:8–9) ‘For the word of God is living and active, sharper than a two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes.’ (Hebrews 4:12–13) Christ, then, gives light to all things and watches over all things. That is why he also said through one of the prophets: ‘I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?’ (Jeremiah 23:23–24) For nothing could escape the mind that knows all things. Or do I not seem to you to have examined this very well?
Palladius: Entirely so.

Cyril: But the prophet saw something unusual about the lampstand, for olive branches were there, and so he asked further: ‘What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on the left? And I asked a second time,’ he says, ‘and said to him, “What are the two branches of the olive trees that are beside the two golden spouts, which pour out and draw up the golden oil vessels?” And he said to me,’ he says, ‘“Do you not know what these are?” And I said, “No, my lord.” And he said to me, “These are the two sons of richness, who stand beside the Lord of all the earth.”’ (Zechariah 4:11–14)
Palladius: Then what need did the blessed prophet have to ask yet again? For he says, ‘I asked a second time’ (Zechariah 4:12).

Cyril: Would you not say, Palladius, that it is wise and fitting for those who have chosen to think rightly in every respect to make their inquiries about any necessary matter precise and carefully refined?
Palladius: I would.

Cyril: Well then: when the prophet saw olive shoots teeming with tender, fresh leaves, he called them olive trees, and not branches from olive trees. Then the divine angel kept silent, waiting for a more thoughtful and…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation: the Zechariah quotation began in s.11 at Zechariah 4:1; the part in this section is 4:3b–5, so the inline citation names only 4:3–5. 'A short account' is the word to Zerubbabel, Zechariah 4:6–10a, which Cyril skips; cited because the reference is unambiguous. 'These are the eyes of the Lord' is Zechariah 4:10b LXX (LXX adds 'seven'; Cyril omits it). Daniel 2:22 follows the Theodotion Greek. Psalm 93:8–9 LXX = Psalm 94:8–9 English. Cyril runs Hebrews 4:12–13 straight on from the Psalm inside one quotation; split into two citations. His Hebrews wording differs from the standard NT text ('sharpened more than a two-edged sword' for 'sharper than any two-edged sword'; 'judging thoughts and notions of the heart'); rendered as he quotes it. 'Shall anything be hidden from me?' is Cyril's loose wording of Jeremiah 23:24 LXX ('If anyone hides in secret places, shall I not see him?'); cited as 23:23–24. 'Christ gives light to all' may echo John 1:9; left uncited as doubtful. LXX 'sons of fatness' (υἱοὶ τῆς πιότητος; Hebrew 'sons of oil', the anointed ones) is rendered 'sons of richness' to keep the oil image Cyril uses in s.13. ἐν ταῖς χερσί ('in the hands of') rendered 'beside', as the LXX idiom means; μυξωτῆρες = spouts (nozzles of the lamps); ἐπαρυστρίδες = oil vessels (lamp funnels). The section ends mid-phrase at the PG column break; the sentence completes in s.13. Κύριε addressed to the angel is rendered 'my lord', lowercase, since it does not mean God; 'the Lord of all the earth' stays capitalised.

title: Olive shoots from Israel and the nations; the bronze altar
english: Cyril: …true question. But when, now roused, he at last named them two branches of olive trees and begged earnestly to learn what these might be symbols of, he was taught at once, when the angel said: ‘These are the two sons of richness, who stand beside the Lord of all the earth’ (Zechariah 4:14). By the two sons of richness he meant the people from Israel and also the people from the nations, who, he says, stand beside the Lord of all the earth. So he clearly and plainly sets the craftsmanship of the lampstand as a type of Christ. Its olive branches, on the right and on the left, having as it were their place all around it, are made rich with the oil, which is a type of the Holy Spirit, who waters the mind of those who believe, as it says: ‘You have anointed my head with oil’ (Psalm 23:5).
Palladius: Then why did he call them shoots of olive trees, and not rather olive trees?

Cyril: Because, my friend, those who have believed have been taken like slender shoots and newly sprouted branches from olive trees, and are all but transplanted, with faith, into godliness: some of them come from the synagogue of the Jews, and others have been taken out of the multitude of the nations. For not all those from Israel have believed, nor has the whole multitude of the nations come in. Branches of olive trees, then, are those who have been plucked, as from trees, from the multitude of the Jews and also of the Greeks, who have come to be in the divine light and already in some way delight in the more abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit. For this, I think, is what is meant by the olive branches lying, as it were, in the spouts of the lamps. The blessed Psalmist also mentions them somewhere, singing to Christ, the Savior of all, and speaking of the bride joined to him, that is, the Church, and of her children in faith: ‘Your wife is like a flourishing vine on the sides of your house; your sons are like young olive plants around your table’ (Psalm 128:3). For we are given life by sharing in the Spirit and at the holy table of Christ, once we have received faith in him.
Palladius: Yes, you are right. For he says, ‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world’ (John 6:33, 51).

Cyril: But let this be what we say for the present about the lampstand and the things on it. Let our discussion now go on to the bronze altar, the most necessary thing in the worship under the law. For he says: ‘You shall make an altar of wood that does not rot, five cubits long and five cubits wide. The altar shall be square, and its height three cubits. And you shall make the horns on the four corners; the horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall cover them with bronze. And you shall make a crown for the altar, and its cover, and its bowls, and its meat forks, and its firepan; all its vessels you shall make of bronze.’ (Exodus 27:1–3) Now, five cubits in breadth and length…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing s.12. Psalm 22:5 LXX = Psalm 23:5 English (ἐλίπανας, 'you made rich/anointed'). Psalm 127:3 LXX = Psalm 128:3 English. Palladius's quotation joins John 6:51 ('I am the living bread that came down from heaven') with John 6:33 ('gives life to the world'); cited as John 6:33, 51. 'Not all those from Israel have believed' and the olive imagery may echo Romans 9:6, 10:16 and 11:17–25; left uncited as doubtful. 'Greeks' (Ἑλληνικῆς) means the pagan nations, as often in Cyril. ἀσήπτων = 'that does not rot' (LXX for acacia wood). In Exodus 27:2 Cyril's text has καλύψεις αὐτά ('cover them'), plural, where the Hebrew has the altar; kept as 'them'. 'Crown' (στεφάνη) and 'cover' (καλυπτήρ) follow the LXX of Exodus 27:3 (Hebrew: pots and shovels). 'Of one piece with it' renders ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἔσται τὰ κέρατα ('the horns shall be from it'). The section ends mid-sentence at the PG column break.

title: Why the altar of the law had no gold
english: Cyril: …was the altar. For it needed, yes, it needed measurements, and very generous ones. For on it were to be brought up split logs and portions of oxen, and whole burnt offerings, and offerings of sheep and goats consecrated to God. That is why its grate and firepan were of bronze, and its meat forks and bowls and all its vessels, so that they could render their own service to the sacrifices of the law and not be destroyed by the assaults of the all-devouring fire. The crown and the horns at the corners we will put down to the beauty of its form, for with the all-wise God nothing is graceless. But come, let us make this point once more, fixing our minds closely on what was decreed about each thing. He ordered an altar suited and fitting for the sacrifices of the law, but there is nothing of gold on it, such as one would certainly see on the ark, and again on the lampstand and the table and the things that go with it.
Palladius: And what, then, does this mean?
Cyril: Did we not say, Palladius, that gold very well signifies the supremacy over all things and the incomparable splendor of the divine and pure nature (splendor as the mind conceives it, I mean)?
Palladius: That is so.

Cyril: Observe, then, that the altar of the worship under the law is entirely without gold. God sets the matter before us as a kind of riddle, and a very clear one: the law in no way procures the Holy Spirit, and the power of the worship in types has not been honored with such a grace. For a spirit of slavery was upon Israel; but to us the gift was granted through Christ after his return to life from the dead. For he breathed on them, saying, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22). That is why Paul also said to those who had believed: ‘For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father”’ (Romans 8:15). And that the power of the worship under the law was not rich in a share of the Holy Spirit, but that this has been given rather to those justified by faith, the wise John will assure us when he says: ‘For the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified’ (John 7:39). For Christ had not yet returned to life; for it was then that human nature was, so to speak, gilded by the Spirit and by fellowship with him. This, then, as I think, is why he ordered the altar to be made without gold. But it seems that to pass over the meaning of the bronze from which it was made would not be without loss for those who love learning. For careful testing may bring forth something needful, as in the saying wisely spoken by someone: ‘In everyone who takes pains there is profit’ (Proverbs 14:23).
Palladius: What, then, could you say about this in turn?

Cyril: Listen, then. Holy Scripture says that the divine Aaron was appointed priest and leader by the decision from above. But Korah and Dathan, and the savage crowd around them, rushing most rashly against the decision from above, and…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing s.13. The printed Σχίσαι is read as σχίζαι ('split logs', the wood for the fire), a noun paired by τε…καί with τμήματα. 'Grate' (ἐσχάρα) is the bronze grating of Exodus 27:4. 'The law in no way procures the Holy Spirit' renders ἥκιστα πρόξενος ('least of all a procurer'). 'A spirit of slavery was upon Israel' anticipates Romans 8:15, quoted next; not cited separately. 'He breathed on them' follows the usual English of John 20:22, where the Greek also has no object. In Romans 8:15 Cyril's text reads 'Abba, the Father' (ὁ Πατήρ); rendered 'Abba, Father'. In 'has been given rather to those justified by faith' the Greek verb is plural (δέδονται) with no expressed subject; rendered with 'this' (the share of the Spirit). John 7:39 is kept literal, 'the Holy Spirit was not yet', as Cyril quotes it. 'With him' (κοινωνίᾳ τῇ πρὸς αὐτόν) is ambiguous between Christ and the Spirit; kept ambiguous. Cyril introduces Proverbs 14:23 LXX (ἐν παντὶ μεριμνῶντι ἔνεστι περισσόν) as 'wisely said by someone'; the Greek of the LXX differs from the Hebrew ('In all toil there is profit'), so it is translated from his wording but cited. Aaron's appointment 'by the decision from above' may refer to Exodus 28:1 or to the budding rod of Numbers 17; left uncited as a general reference. The section ends mid-sentence at the PG column break.

title: Korah's firepans and the bronze altar; the altar of incense
english: Cyril: …rising up against the divine laws, brought firepans uninvited, going to this of their own accord and seizing an honor not assigned to them; and out of madness and audacity they drew up their ranks with great heat against the priest who stood first and had been chosen out from all the others (Numbers 16:1–18). Through these events the madness that the Jews would later show against Christ was sketched in outline. For he himself is our High Priest, brought to this by the decision of the Father. Those men paid the penalty for such shameful attempts, and after them the Jews too will pay it, since they have become liable to the same charges. Then God said to holy Moses, and also to Eleazar the priest, the son of Aaron: ‘Take up the bronze firepans from among those who were burned, and scatter this strange fire there, for the firepans of these sinners have become holy at the cost of their lives. And they made them into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, because they had been offered before the Lord and were made holy. And they became a sign to the sons of Israel.’ (Numbers 16:37–38) This is what God said at that time. And in Exodus it is written about Bezalel, whose father was Uri and whose tribe was Dan, and who led in every kind of skilled craft: ‘He made the bronze altar from the bronze firepans that belonged to the men who rebelled with the company of Korah’ (Exodus 38:22, Septuagint).
Palladius: What, then, does this mean?

Cyril: It would be of great benefit if one considered that the ark was made as a type of Christ, and so too were the other things, I mean the lampstand and the mercy seat and the table of gold, when the people brought their offerings and each one dedicated what he had in hand. For those who bear fruit for Christ and bring spiritual offerings are very acceptable, to the glory of God the Father; and those people of old were types and shadows of them. But the altar of the worship under the law is shown, mystically and by God’s design, to be a kind of memorial and proclamation in advance, lying in its very construction, of the provocation and defiance, and, if I may now put it so, the revolt, that arose against the great priest. Is the riddle clear to you? For Aaron stands as a type of Christ; and the Jews too contended against the glory of Christ, and for this reason the altar under the law is spoken against. For the worship as in shadows has ceased, and in Christ instead we give forth to the Father a spiritual fragrance. And this too he sketched for us beforehand, again as in shadows, when he said: ‘And you shall make for me an altar of incense of wood that does not rot; you shall make it a cubit long and a cubit wide. It shall be square, and two cubits high. Its horns shall be of one piece with it. And you shall overlay it with pure gold: its grate, and its walls all around, and its horns.’ (Exodus 30:1–3) Then, after adding poles and rings and carrying bars for it, and other such things (Exodus 30:4–5), ‘you shall set it,’ he says, ‘before the…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, completing s.14 (the grammar of the Korah sentence is loose in Greek: dative τοῖς ἀμφ’ αὐτούς with nominative participles; rendered as one subject). The Korah narrative (Korah and Dathan, firepans, seizing the priesthood) is paraphrased from Numbers 16:1–18 and cited there; Abiram is not named. 'Brought to this by the decision of the Father' likely echoes Hebrews 5:4–5; left uncited as not verbal. The firepan command is LXX Numbers 17:2–3 = English Numbers 16:37–38 (LXX 17:1–15 = English 16:36–50). Cyril's text has ἡγίασε (singular) where Rahlfs has ἡγίασαν; read with τὰ πυρεῖα as its neuter-plural subject (singular verb by rule), 'the firepans have become holy', which matches the Hebrew ('for they are holy') and the following ἡγιάσθησαν. ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς αὐτῶν ('in their souls') rendered 'at the cost of their lives', its sense in the Hebrew and LXX. His text has 'they made them' (ἐποίησαν) where the LXX has the command 'make them' (ποίησον); kept as he quotes it. The verse about Bezalel making the bronze altar from Korah's firepans exists only in the Septuagint (Exodus 38:22 in the LXX, Brenton 38:22; no counterpart in the Hebrew or English Bible, whose bronze altar is Exodus 38:1–7); hence the citation 'Exodus 38:22, Septuagint'. Cyril says Bezalel was of the tribe of Dan; Exodus 31:2 and 38:22 (English) make him of Judah, and Oholiab of Dan (Exodus 31:6). Translated as Cyril wrote it; the slip is his or his text's. 'The people brought their offerings and each dedicated what he had in hand' refers to Exodus 25:1–8 and 35:20–29; left uncited as a general reference. 'Those people of old' renders the masculine ἐκεῖνοι (the Israelite givers); ὧν could also mean the offerings. 'Defiance' (ἀντιλογία, 'speaking against', echoed by ἀντιλέγεται 'is spoken against' just after) may recall Jude 11 ('the rebellion of Korah'); 'we give forth to the Father the spiritual fragrance' may recall 2 Corinthians 2:15; both left uncited as doubtful. νοητός ('perceived by the mind') rendered 'spiritual'. οἰκονομικῶς rendered 'by God's design'. The incense altar's 'grate' (ἐσχάρα) follows the LXX of Exodus 30:3 (Hebrew: its top). The poles, rings and carrying bars summarise Exodus 30:4–5. The quotation of Exodus 30:6–10 begins at the end and continues in s.16, mid-word (καταπε|τάσματος, 'before the | veil'); its citation belongs to s.16.

title: The incense altar as a figure of Christ
english: Cyril: …the veil that is over the ark of the testimony, from which I will make myself known to you. And Aaron shall burn on it compound incense, finely ground, morning by morning; whenever he shades the lamps, he shall burn incense on it. And when Aaron lights the lamps in the evening, he shall burn incense on it, a perpetual incense, continually before the Lord throughout their generations. You shall offer no other incense on it, no burnt offering of sacrifice, and you shall pour no drink offering on it. And Aaron shall make atonement on it, on its horns, once a year, with the blood of the cleansing from sins, the blood of atonement. Once a year he shall cleanse it throughout their generations. It is most holy to the Lord.’ (Exodus 30:6–10)
Palladius: Are we to take this too, then, as a type of Christ?

Cyril: Certainly, Palladius. For in truth the thing would quite readily show its precious and deep mystery to those who choose to study such things closely and with exact care. The altar was made of wood that does not decay, and it was overlaid entirely with gold (Exodus 30:1, 3). For the body of Christ is incorruptible, and it is rich in the divine nature it holds within itself: ‘For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14). Christ is our firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the root of our race as it is created anew for incorruption through union with God, even if in his case this must be understood in a unique sense. The altar also has horns, like outstretched hands, and these prefigure the shape of the precious cross. If someone should say that there are four horns, that does the lover of learning no harm in understanding the matter rightly. For since the altar is square and equal on every side, the horns look the same from every side. And what does this mean? In every place Christ is known, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2); and this is a splendid boast for those who believe in him. So the inspired Paul says: ‘But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Galatians 6:14). A twisted crown is added to the work as an ornament (Exodus 30:3), for Emmanuel is truly ‘fair in beauty beyond the sons of men’ (Psalm 45:2). The things it needed were also provided, the carrying poles and the rest (Exodus 30:4–5). For the divine altar had to be carried in good order at the times of breaking camp. The inspired disciples did this too, carrying Christ about through their preaching, fittingly and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40), as servants of God (2 Corinthians 6:4) and stewards of the mysteries of Christ (1 Corinthians 4:1). ‘And you shall set the altar,’ he says, ‘opposite the veil that is over the ark of the testimonies, from which I will make myself known to you’ (Exodus 30:6).
Palladius: Then what need was there, I wonder, for the places assigned to them?
Cyril: How deep this subject is, and how very obscure! Still, I will speak as best I can, trusting in God, who makes wise even…
translator_notes: The opening paragraphs continue the Exodus 30:1-10 quotation begun at the end of section 15 (Cyril is still speaking); the citation (Exodus 30:6–10) covers the part quoted in this section. Text reads 'γνωσθήσομαί σοι ἐκεῖ Θεός'; LXX and Cyril's own repetition at the end of the section read 'ἐκεῖθεν', so translated 'from there' (likely OCR/print corruption). Cyril's text reads 'ἐπισκιάζῃ τοὺς λύχνους' (shades the lamps) where standard LXX has 'ἐπισκευάζῃ' (trims/dresses); kept 'shades' because Cyril's exegesis in section 18 builds on 'lit and shaded'. 'κάρπωμα θυσίας' rendered 'burnt offering of sacrifice' (LXX κάρπωμα normally = whole/burnt offering); the Hebrew of 30:9 lists burnt offering and grain offering separately. 'Ἀληθὲς γὰρ ὅτι τὸ χρῆμά ἐστι...' is syntactically awkward and possibly corrupt; rendered by sense ('in truth the thing would show'). 'ἐνδείξ[ει]εν' and 'ἀλήλ[ε]ιπτο' are editorial brackets in the print, read as ἐνδείξειεν, ἀλήλιπτο. Exodus 30:2-3 names 'its horns' without a number; Cyril concedes the reader may count four. Psalm 45:2 = LXX Psalm 44:3. 'ἐν κόσμῳ' (carried 'in good order') could also mean 'in the world'; chose 'order' because the next clause pairs it with 'becomingly and in order' (echo of 1 Corinthians 14:40); doubtful. 1 Corinthians 4:1 reads 'stewards of the mysteries of God'; Cyril has 'of Christ'. 'Θεοῦ διάκονοι' = 2 Corinthians 6:4 wording. Palladius' question 'τί τὸ ἀναγκαῖον καὶ χώρων αὐτῶν οἶμαι, τῶν τεταγμένων' is corrupt as printed; rendered by sense (why each piece is placed where it is). Section ends mid-sentence; the verb's object 'the blind' (Psalm 146:8) opens section 17. 'Firstfruits' cited to 1 Corinthians 15:20 (also 15:23). 'καὶ οὗτος ἐσταυρωμένος' echoes 1 Corinthians 2:2 ('καὶ τοῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον').

title: The ark below and the mercy seat above
english: Cyril: …the blind (Psalm 146:8). He says that an ark was to be made of wood that does not decay and of pure gold, and the law was in it, that is, the divine word, or the testimonies (Exodus 25:10–11, 16). For the thing was a type of the Word who was born of God, who dwelt among us (John 1:14) and came in the likeness of flesh (Romans 8:3; Philippians 2:7), according to the Scriptures. Then he said that a veil stretched on four pillars must hang before the ark (Exodus 26:31–33). And the name given to the veil is the mercy seat. This too is Christ. ‘For he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1 John 2:2), ‘and a mercy seat through faith’ (Romans 3:25); for so Paul named him. The cherubim, too, were depicted, as it were, around the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18–20). They signify very well that the highest powers serve under God, for the Word is God (John 1:1); that they are very near, and indeed that they stand in attendance as ministers. Then God said to Moses: ‘And I will make myself known to you from there, and I will speak to you from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony’ (Exodus 25:22). Now the ark, as I said, was Christ, God the Word in an incorruptible body; but the ark was set on the ground, and the Only-begotten entered the low and humble state that is ours. For he took on the form of a slave and emptied himself (Philippians 2:7). Yet he himself is also the mercy seat, which lies on high and is escorted by the powers above. For the Son is made known to us not only by the ways in which he emptied himself, but also by all that makes him God and Lord of all. Even though he humbled himself on account of his humanity (Philippians 2:8), coming down, in the divine plan, into our condition, still ‘God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name’ (Philippians 2:9). And this too has its type: the mercy seat was set on high, with the cherubim depicted on its right and its left. For where the service fit for God alone is seen, there surely must also be the glory of the Godhead and a dignity supreme beyond words. ‘And from above the cherubim I will make myself known to you’ (Exodus 25:22), says the Master of all. He commands that the ineffable nature be sought not among created things, but wholly beyond whatever has been called into being. For the most fitting way to think of God’s nature, and the most fitting place for it, is what lies beyond and above everything that has come into being. So the place above the cherubim, even in visible form in the holy tent, all but shows us the divine nature. That is why he commanded that the golden altar, made as a type of Christ, be set opposite the one who gives his oracles from above the cherubim and is understood to be there (Exodus 30:6). This signifies, I think, that in Christ our affairs came, as it were, into God’s sight and before the eyes of the Father. For man had turned away and had offended God by the transgression and by much sin, and Christ set him again before the face of the Father, in himself, as the first. ‘For as a forerunner he has entered heaven on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), now to appear in the presence of God for us’ (Hebrews 9:24), as the wise Paul writes to us. For he who always exists with his own…
translator_notes: 'τοὺς τυφλούς' completes the clause at the end of section 16 ('God who makes wise even the blind'): LXX Psalm 145:8 'κύριος σοφοῖ τυφλούς' = English Psalm 146:8 (Hebrew 'opens the eyes of the blind'). Ark: Exodus 25:10–11, 16 in English numbering (LXX Exodus 25:9–10, 15 in Rahlfs-style numbering). 'Likeness of flesh' echoes Romans 8:3 (Cyril omits 'of sin') and Philippians 2:7 ('γενόμενος ἐν ὁμοιώματι'). Cyril says the veil itself is named 'mercy seat' (ἱλαστήριον); in Exodus 25:17 the ἱλαστήριον is the lid of the ark, not the veil of 26:31–33. Translated as written, not harmonised. The double quotation joins 1 John 2:2 ('ἱλασμός') and Romans 3:25 ('ἱλαστήριον διὰ πίστεως'); 'so Paul named him' refers to the second. 'Θεὸς γὰρ ὁ Λόγος' = John 1:1. 'πλὴν εἰς γῆν ἡ κιβωτός' is elliptic (no verb): rendered 'the ark was set on the ground'. Exodus 25:22 = LXX 25:21. 'In himself, as the first' renders 'ὡς ἐν ἑαυτῷ καὶ πρώτῳ' (Christ as first of the restored race). The Hebrews quotation fuses 6:20 ('πρόδρομος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν') and 9:24 ('νῦν ἐμφανισθῆναι τῷ προσώπῳ τοῦ θεοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν'); Cyril ascribes Hebrews to Paul, kept as he wrote it. 'The service... as ministers' may echo Hebrews 1:14 (λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα); uncited as doubtful. Section ends mid-sentence; 'Father' opens section 18.

title: Christ the compound and fine incense
english: Cyril: …Father, is said ‘now to appear,’ because in himself, as the first, he sets human nature in the Father’s sight and removes that ancient turning away. ‘For he is our peace’ (Ephesians 2:14), as the Scriptures say.
Palladius: So it is settled that the golden altar is again an image of Christ.

Cyril: And besides this, he himself may fittingly be understood as the compound and fine incense. For he himself is the high priest: ‘For Aaron,’ he says, ‘shall burn on it compound, fine incense’ (Exodus 30:7). The incense is compound, for the Word, being God, became flesh (John 1:14). Emmanuel is in a way compounded for us, divine nature and humanity being brought together, beyond words, into a unity beyond understanding. And it is fine, because it has nothing of the coarseness of worship under the law. ‘For sacrifices and offering you did not desire; in burnt offering and sin offering you took no pleasure. But a body you prepared for me,’ he says; ‘then I said, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God’ (Hebrews 10:5–7; Psalm 40:6–8). And what this will of the Father is, he himself has taught us in the Gospels, saying: ‘I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day’ (John 6:38–39). For he offered himself for us as a fragrant aroma, and for this reason he was also named high priest. So he himself is the high priest, and he himself is the compound and fine incense. Paul will bear witness, saying: ‘But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and through us reveals the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place. For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some a fragrance from death to death, to others a fragrance of life to life’ (2 Corinthians 2:14–16). And he called to us as well: ‘Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God as a fragrant aroma’ (Ephesians 5:1–2). He also fixed a clear time for burning incense, laying down that everything must be done in order and with propriety, and by means that would make plain to us the force of the insights that point inward. ‘In the morning,’ he says, ‘and in the evening, when the lamps are lit and shaded’ (Exodus 30:7–8). The evening and the morning show what is unceasing and continual. The need to burn incense by lamplight perhaps hints very well at this: when we are lit by the divine light, it is then, truly then, that we are richly filled with the fragrance of Christ, and so we come to perceive the good things within the tent, that is, the distribution of the divine gifts of grace that Christ holds out to the worthy. So if anyone has not yet come into the light through faith, he surely has no share in the spiritual fragrance either, since he does not yet know the mystery of Christ.
translator_notes: Opening sentence completes section 17 ('he who always exists with his own Father is said "now to appear"'), picking up Hebrews 9:24, which is cited in section 17; not re-cited here. 'For he is our peace' = Ephesians 2:14. 'τὰ ἀνθρώπινα' (the human things) rendered 'human nature'; could also be 'human affairs'. The Psalm quotation follows the Hebrews 10:5–7 form ('a body you prepared', with 'θυσίας καὶ προσφοράν'), with the clauses in Cyril's own order (burnt offering line before 'a body'); Hebrew/English Psalm 40:6–8 = LXX Psalm 39:7–9; the Hebrew has 'ears you have dug' for 'a body'. 'Θυσίας' may be accusative plural or genitive; rendered as the Hebrews singular sense 'sacrifice'. 'Fragrant aroma' (εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας) in 'he offered himself for us' anticipates Ephesians 5:2, quoted in full below; not cited separately. 'κεχρημάτικε... ἀρχιερεύς' (was styled high priest) may echo Hebrews 5:10; uncited as doubtful. 'ἐν τάξει τε καὶ εὐκοσμίᾳ' is near 1 Corinthians 14:40 in sense but not in wording; uncited. 'Lit and shaded': Cyril's text of Exodus 30:7–8 has ἐπισκιάζω (see note at section 16; LXX standard ἐπισκευάζω, 'trims'). 'νοητὴ εὐωδία' rendered 'spiritual fragrance' (fragrance perceived by the mind). 'ἴμεν' read as 1st plural of εἶμι ('we go/come'). Cyril's text of 2 Corinthians 2:16 reads 'ὀσμὴ ζωῆς εἰς ζωήν' (no ἐκ), so 'of life to life'. 'ὑπὸ λύχνοις' read as 'by lamplight' (while the lamps burn).

title: No other incense than Christ; the false fragrance of the Antichrist
english: Cyril: ‘For if you do not believe, neither will you understand,’ (Isaiah 7:9) he says. For faith is the first approach that leads on to understanding, and it opens the mind, as it were, to receive the divine light. He calls the incense ‘perpetual’ (Exodus 30:8), for there is no time when Christ does not give off his fragrance in the holy tent, that is, in the Church. And he altogether forbids any drink offering to be poured out on it, or any burnt offering to be offered up on it (Exodus 30:9), meaning, clearly, on the altar, which is Christ.
