For in Christ the things of the law have been abolished, and the shadows are drawing to their end. That, I think, is what the drink offering and the burnt offering stand for. The prophet bears witness when he says, ‘Sacrifice and drink offering have been taken away from the house of the Lord’ (Joel 1:9). For now that worship and service in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24) have been revealed, the shadows are in a sense superfluous, and whatever is done in types is futile and wholly useless; for in Christ there is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). For those who would be justified in the law after the truth has been revealed have fallen away from grace (Galatians 5:4). ‘You shall not offer,’ he says, ‘other incense on the altar’ (Exodus 30:9). For in Christ we will accept no other whatever. We will call no one at all ‘Rabbi,’ for we have one Teacher and Master (Matthew 23:8–10), and to him alone we will hold fast, saying, ‘Your name is perfume poured out; therefore the maidens have loved you. They drew me; they ran after you toward the fragrance of your perfumes’ (Song of Songs 1:3–4). Or is this not what is meant by ‘You shall not offer other incense on it’ (Exodus 30:9)? For to those who are truly sensible, the fragrance of Christ alone in the Church would be enough; they long for no other scent, whereas the wretched Jews certainly do. For in their folly they heap insults on the compounded and finely ground incense, that is, on Christ. They have remained without any share in this sacred, or rather truly divine, fragrance; but they will receive another in his place, the son of lawlessness, ‘who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God,’ as it is written, ‘proclaiming himself to be God’ (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). He also defiles the divine tent, since he is foreign smoke and, if I may put it so, a devilish stench. ‘For his coming,’ it says, ‘will be by the working of Satan’ (2 Thessalonians 2:9).
Palladius: I understand what you mean, for the argument is plain.

Cyril: Further, he commands Aaron to make atonement on the altar of incense once a year, smearing the tips of its horns with the blood of the purification of sins. ‘For it is,’ he says, ‘holy of holies’ (Exodus 30:10). The inspired Paul will make this clear to you when he says: ‘But when Christ came as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, not through the blood of goats and bulls but through his own blood, he entered once for all into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption’ (Hebrews 9:11–12).
translator_notes: Isaiah 7:9 is the LXX reading ('you will not understand'); the Hebrew has 'you will not stand firm'. The section ends mid-word in the Greek (εὑ|ράμενος, Hebrews 9:12); the whole participle 'having obtained eternal redemption' is rendered here, so §20 opens with Romans 6. Exodus 30:9 LXX reads 'You shall not offer other incense on it, a burnt offering, a sacrifice; and you shall not pour a drink offering on it'; Cyril paraphrases the libation and burnt-offering clause before quoting the incense clause twice. 'Son of lawlessness' blends 2 Thessalonians 2:3 ('man of lawlessness ... son of perdition'); the cite covers 2:3-4. 'They will receive another in his place' may echo John 5:43; left uncited as doubtful. 'Abolished in Christ' may echo 2 Corinthians 3:14; left uncited. Cyril's Song of Songs text has 'they drew me ... having run' where Rahlfs LXX has 'they drew you ... we will run'; rendered as Cyril has it. LXX and English verse numbers agree for Song of Songs 1:3-4. 'Wretched' renders τάλανες in Cyril's anti-Jewish polemic; kept as written, not softened or sharpened. 'Holy of holies' (Exodus 30:10, 'most holy') is kept literal because §20 builds on it ('Christ ... the Holy of Holies by nature'). μόσχων in Hebrews 9:12 is rendered 'bulls' to match the μόσχος of Leviticus 4 that §20 reads against it.

title: Christ the altar, the incense, the priest and the cleansing blood
english: Cyril: For, as he says again elsewhere, ‘Having died once, he dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God’ (Romans 6:9–10). The revered Aaron, then, used to enter the Holy of Holies once a year with the blood of the purification of sins (Leviticus 16:34; Hebrews 9:7). See Christ again in these things, all but sprinkling his own cross with his own blood, the blood that is the salvation and life of all. For the horns are a figure of the cross, jutting out on this side and that, like arms stretched wide. Understand, then, that Christ died once, and that he is the Holy of Holies by nature, as God. For John speaks the truth when he says, ‘From his fullness we have all received’ (John 1:16). For all creation, visible and invisible, has its share in Christ. Angels and archangels, and the beings higher still, and even the Cherubim themselves, are holy in no other way than through Christ alone, in the Holy Spirit. So he himself is the altar; he is the incense and the High Priest; and he likewise is the blood of the purification of sins.
Palladius: Yes, you are right. But what the blood of the purification of sins actually is, I cannot clearly grasp.

Cyril: The law was sketching in advance the cleansing through blood and the holy victim, Christ I mean, through whom we have been saved, escaping the defilement that sin had worked deep into us. It speaks somewhat like this in Leviticus: ‘If the whole congregation of Israel errs unwittingly, and a matter escapes the eyes of the congregation, and they do any one of the things that the commandments of the Lord say must not be done, and so transgress, and the sin they have committed becomes known to them, then the congregation shall bring a young bull from the herd, without blemish, as a sin offering, and bring it to the doors of the tent of witness. And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the bull before the Lord, and they shall slaughter the bull before the Lord. And the anointed priest shall bring some of the bull’s blood into the tent of witness. The priest shall dip his finger in the bull’s blood and sprinkle it seven times before the Lord, in front of the veil of the sanctuary. And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of compounded incense, which is before the Lord in the tent of witness’ (Leviticus 4:13–18). We will speak about these things more fully in due course. But see Emmanuel again, slain for us as in the bull, freeing us from sin, taking us out of the reach of judgment and carrying us away from punishment, and passing through the greater and more perfect tent, not by bulls and goats but by his own blood (Hebrews 9:11–12), having tasted death once for all. For up on the wood, when his side was pierced with a spear, he poured out blood and water (John 19:34). And the projecting horns would be a figure of the cross, as we said before.
translator_notes: The Greek section opens with the last letters of εὑράμενος (Hebrews 9:12), rendered at the end of §19. Cyril's Romans 6:9 reads 'having died once' where the New Testament text has 'having been raised from the dead'; translated as Cyril quotes it. 'Once a year with the blood of the purification of sins' echoes the wording of Exodus 30:10 and Leviticus 16:34 and the summary in Hebrews 9:7; cited to Leviticus 16:34 and Hebrews 9:7. The Leviticus quotation is 4:13-18a (it stops before 'and he shall pour out the rest of the blood'). 'The anointed priest' renders ὁ ἱερεὺς ὁ χριστός, lower case because it names the high priest of the law. μόσχος is rendered 'young bull' / 'bull' throughout, matching Leviticus 4 and Hebrews 9 ('calves' in many English Bibles of Hebrews 9:12). 'All creation, visible and invisible' may echo Colossians 1:16; left uncited. 'Having tasted death' may echo Hebrews 2:9; left uncited. δίκη is rendered 'judgment' (it can also mean 'penalty').

title: The bronze laver: cleansing by water, a figure of baptism
english: Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: Yet the law, speaking in riddles, did not order cleansing by blood alone; it also commanded cleansing with holy water. For this is the most perfect path to cleansing, according to the mystery that is in Christ.
Palladius: And how has it shown this as well, or in what way?

Cyril: It is written: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Make a bronze laver, with its base of bronze, for washing. You shall set it between the tent of witness and the altar, and you shall pour water into it. Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet from it with water. Whenever they go into the tent of witness, they shall wash with water, and they will not die; or whenever they approach the altar to minister and to offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord, they shall wash their hands and their feet with water. Whenever they go into the tent of witness, they shall wash with water so that they may not die; and it shall be a perpetual ordinance for them, for him and for his generations after him’ (Exodus 30:17–21). It is plain enough, then, that the grace given through holy baptism was being sketched in advance here. For when we are baptized, what we gain is not the removal of dirt from the flesh (1 Peter 3:21); rather, we are set free from the defilements of mind and heart, and we wash away the stains of our offenses, by the grace and loving-kindness of the One who calls us to salvation. For we have been justified not by works of the law, as the Scriptures say, but by faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 2:16). Now see how Aaron, though he was holy according to the law, and those appointed to minister with him as well, first wash their hands and feet with water, and only then set their hands to the sacred tasks and run into the Holy of Holies free from fear. Here, I think, the law shows plainly and clearly, and the fact itself all but cries out, that even one who seems to be consecrated according to the law is unconsecrated before God unless he washes in the water, and that the power of worship under the law is not enough for cleansing. At any rate, they washed beforehand, even though they had been sanctified according to the law; and what is cleansed is surely not what is clean, but what is dirty and unclean. Christ himself said something of this kind: ‘One who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, for he is clean’ (John 13:10). And the most wise Paul writes that it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). So the law falls short of sanctification unless saving baptism is added for those who thirst for closeness to God. That is why the blessed John too, though richly crowned with the highest honors, and though he knew how to advance so far in virtue that he had already reached the highest rank, begged the Savior to baptize him, saying, ‘I need to be baptized by you’ (Matthew 3:14).
Palladius: True.
Cyril: The washing of hands and feet signifies purity and sincerity in what we do and in our course, so to speak, toward each of our duties.
translator_notes: The Greek section ends mid-sentence (ἔργου καὶ πορείας ... πρὸς ἕκαστα τῶν πρακτέων,); its object and verb, τὸ καθαρὸν καὶ ἀκίβδηλον ὑποσημαίνουσιν, open §22. English needs the verb early, so the whole sentence is rendered at the end of §21 and §22 begins with the next sentence. Cyril's Exodus 30:17-21 follows the LXX, which repeats the 'whenever they go into the tent' clause; kept. 'Holy water' renders ὕδατι τῷ ἁγίῳ (the cleansing water of the laver read as baptism), not the later sacramental 'holy water'. ἱερός / ἀνίερος are rendered 'consecrated / unconsecrated' to keep Cyril's wordplay. 'Saying, I need to be baptized by you' follows Matthew 3:14; Cyril's 'begged the Savior to be baptized' is rendered 'begged the Savior to baptize him'. 'The law falls short of sanctification' may echo Hebrews 7:19 ('the law made nothing perfect'); left uncited. Cyril calls the author of Hebrews 'Paul', as in the rest of the work.

title: Cleansed before approaching God; the laver made from mirrors
english: Cyril: Once we have trained ourselves in this, we are allowed to enter the inner tent, to bring spiritual sacrifices to God (1 Peter 2:5), and, as if in place of incense, to consecrate in a sense the sweet fragrance of the Gospel way of life. And he gives the useful instruction that those who wish to go into the Holy of Holies, and those who have charge of the sacred works, must wash, so that they may not die (Exodus 30:20–21). For it is a perilous and truly harmful thing to draw near to God without being cleansed. That is why the wise Paul charges us, if we wish to share in the mystical blessing, to examine ourselves and only then to come forward (1 Corinthians 11:28). And he reveals that carelessness in these matters is full of danger, when he says, ‘That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world’ (1 Corinthians 11:30–32).
Palladius: It is settled, then, that the sacred laver pointed in advance to the grace that comes to us through holy baptism.

Cyril: So it is; do not doubt it at all. And if you look closely at how it was made, you will, I think, be still more amazed. For this is written about Bezalel, who crafted the furnishings of the tent: ‘He made the bronze laver and its bronze base from the mirrors of the women who fasted, who fasted at the doors of the tent of witness on the day he pitched it’ (Exodus 38:8). ‘And he made the laver so that Moses and Aaron and his sons might wash their hands and their feet from it when they went into the tent of witness; whenever they approached the altar to minister, they washed from it, just as the Lord had commanded Moses’ (Exodus 40:31–32).
Palladius: And what is this matter of the mirrors? And who were the women who fasted?

Cyril: Many things that took place are not clearly narrated in divine Scripture; they are indicated somehow in passing, as is indeed the case with the matter before us. For Moses did not say where the women fasted, or who they were, when the holy tent had been set up. But that it happened, no one could doubt, for it is stated, even if not clearly. But let us leave this and go on to that other point, if you agree.
Palladius: Which point?
Cyril: What might the women who fasted be a figure of? And what does it mean that the bronze laver was shaped from the mirrors?
Palladius: Well, it is for you to tell me this too.

Cyril: Listen, then. The Israelites served idols while they endured slavery under the Egyptians, and they spent long years living by the Egyptians’ laws. Now it was a custom among the Egyptians, especially for the women, to go regularly to the temples dressed in linen garments, solemnly adorned with a mirror in the left hand and a sistrum in the right; these were women who,
translator_notes: The Greek section opens with τὸ καθαρὸν καὶ ἀκίβδηλον ὑποσημαίνουσιν, which completes the last sentence of §21 and is rendered there. The section ends mid-sentence: the relative αἳ ὅτι ('women who, as ...') is left for §23, whose Greek continues μάλιστα τῶν ἄλλων ἐξειλεγμέναι; the relative is now rendered at the end of §22 ('these were women who,'), so the §23 English ('…chosen out above all the others ... were barely counted worthy') completes it; ὅτι μάλιστα is the idiom 'most especially'. The Bezalel quotation is LXX Exodus 38:26-27 (Rahlfs). Its first sentence matches Hebrew/English Exodus 38:8, where the women 'served' or 'ministered' at the entrance (LXX 'fasted'); Cyril's argument rests on the LXX 'fasted', so that is kept. Its second sentence has no counterpart in Hebrew chapter 38 but matches Exodus 40:31-32, so it is cited there. 'The mystical blessing' (μυστικὴ εὐλογία) is Cyril's usual name for the Eucharist; kept as written. Cyril's 1 Corinthians 11:31 reads ἐκρίνομεν where the New Testament text has διεκρίνομεν; the sense 'judged ourselves' is the same. 'Spiritual sacrifices' (θυσίας πνευματικάς) matches 1 Peter 2:5 word for word, so it is cited. 'Served idols ... in Egypt' may echo Joshua 24:14 or Ezekiel 20:7-8; left uncited as doubtful. 'Sistrum' is the Egyptian rattle used in the cult of Isis; kept as the plain English name of the instrument.

title: The mirrors of the fasting women, and the tent itself
english: Cyril: …chosen out above all the others and initiated into the rites, were barely counted worthy of such an honor, or rather of such an outrage, for that is the better and truer word. So some women of Israel’s blood found among their own belongings these remnants of the worship in Egypt, and they brought these very mirrors as an offering, and the mirrors were made over into the laver (Exodus 38:8). When the holy tent had been set up, they fasted, sitting somewhere by its doors and living purely in everything (Exodus 38:8). The event hints, I think, at this: once the truer tent had been revealed, that is, the Church, which the Lord pitched, and not man, as the inspired Paul writes (Hebrews 8:2), it is now, in a way, time for those once devoted to the glory of the herd of demons to be remade into holy vessels, fit to receive holy baptism, so that they too could shine with glories beyond the law. For this, I think, is what it means that the bronze laver was fashioned out of pagan mirrors, that is, out of the devil’s treasures. In it is the water that cleansed even Moses himself (Exodus 40:31) and served the priesthood under the law for washing (Exodus 30:19–21), a washing plainly to be understood spiritually. Or would you not say yourself, Palladius, that those who have gone astray and worshipped demons are vessels of the devil?
Palladius: How could I not?

Cyril: The women fasted beside the doors of the holy tent. This too would be a fine and wise riddle. It shows that those who have been justified in Christ do not hurry into the churches by means of blood, but are distinguished rather by spiritual sacrifices, and bring to God, as a kind of gift, their self-control, which is, so to speak, a putting to death of the flesh. For he says: ‘Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable worship’ (Romans 12:1). And again: ‘Glorify God in your body’ (1 Corinthians 6:20). So the women who fasted when the holy tent had been set up stand as an image of souls that are no longer schooled by the commandments of Moses, but have already shown forth a spiritual and gospel way of life. Such souls tread down earthly pleasures, not without sweat, and are being thoroughly reshaped toward a beauty without stain, because they will not bear to fall into the foul and profane offences of love of the flesh. Or is this not the manner of life for us who have been called in Christ to sanctification and spiritual leanness?
Palladius: It certainly is.

Cyril: Let this be enough for now about the holy vessels. Come, if you agree, let us also look closely at the tent itself, how it was placed and how it was built. The matter is deep and beyond our measure. Yet I think there is no harm at all in our being eager to gather from every side what makes for our profit, and in reaching, as far as we can, toward things that lie far above us.
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence, continuing Cyril’s account (end of s.22) of Egyptian priestesses carrying a mirror and a sistrum; ‘ὅτι μάλιστα’ is split across the break and taken with ‘chosen out above all the others’. The mirrors of the women who fasted at the doors of the tent: LXX Exodus 38:26 = English Exodus 38:8; the LXX reads ‘fasted’ (νηστευσασῶν) where the Hebrew has ‘served/ministered’, which is why Cyril speaks of fasting. ‘Ἑλληνικῶν’ rendered ‘pagan’ (Cyril’s usual sense). The water that ‘cleansed even Moses’ refers to Exodus 40:31 (Moses, Aaron and his sons washed at the laver); Exodus 30:19–21 for the priests’ washing. ‘θυσίαις πνευματικαῖς’ echoes 1 Peter 2:5 and ‘κεκλημένοις εἰς ἁγιασμόν’ echoes 1 Thessalonians 4:7; both left uncited as general phrasing. ‘νέκρωσις τῆς σαρκός’ may echo Colossians 3:5 / 2 Corinthians 4:10; uncited. ‘ἰσχνότης’ (leanness, i.e. the thinness of fasting) kept as ‘spiritual leanness’.

title: The ten curtains: the churches joined in one
english: Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: If someone chose to treat it in very fine detail, the discussion of each point would grow long and branch in many directions. But one should know that some features belong to the vessels and lie close to contemplation and mystical meanings, while others were devised for the adornment and use of the tent. So I will cut the length of the discussion as far as I can, speak briefly, and keep the account short. He said, then: ‘You shall make the tent with ten curtains of twisted linen, blue, purple and twisted scarlet. You shall make them with Cherubim, the work of a weaver. The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and the width of one curtain four cubits; all the curtains shall have the same measure. Five curtains shall be joined to one another, one to the other, and five curtains shall be joined, one to the other’ (Exodus 26:1–3). So there are ten curtains, and they are closely fastened to one another. For there are many dwelling places with the Father (John 14:2), and all who dwell in them have one holy aim, and one knowledge of God. For God has called us in peace, as it is written (1 Corinthians 7:15). If you like, you may take the ten curtains and consider them to be the full number of the churches throughout the world, not scattered into dissension or discordant opinion, but united in spirit and, as it were, bound tightly into one in the unity that is in Christ through faith. For everywhere and in all of them there is ‘one Lord, one faith, one baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5). Each of the curtains is four cubits wide and twenty-eight long (Exodus 26:2). The riddle is intricate and subtle, but I think it shows, darkly and dimly, that even the training given through the law is in some way accepted in the churches. It is very narrow, because the letter is obscure; yet as time stretches on in length, it will have as its end the mystery of Christ, that is, the eighth, the resurrection that took place on the eighth day. For Christ is the end of the law (Romans 10:4) and of the prophets, and to him the divine David cried aloud: ‘Your commandment is exceedingly broad’ (Psalm 119:96). The inspired Paul also writes to those who had valued worship under the law above faith in Christ: ‘Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return (I speak as to children), be enlarged yourselves as well. Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers’ (2 Corinthians 6:11–14). Do you see that wanting to attach oneself to the Jews who disobeyed, who still speak the things of the law now that faith has come, makes people restricted?
Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: The cloth of the curtains is of twisted linen, blue, purple and twisted scarlet (Exodus 26:1). For the adornment of the Church is richly varied. This is what the inspired David also sings, speaking somewhere of her in this way (Psalm 45:9): ‘The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a robe woven with gold,
translator_notes: Exodus 26:1–3 quoted from the LXX (same numbering in English Bibles). ὑάκινθος rendered ‘blue’ (the tabernacle colour; LXX ‘hyacinth’). ‘Many dwelling places with the Father’ is a clear allusion to John 14:2 (μοναί). ‘In peace God has called us’ is introduced with ‘as it is written’: 1 Corinthians 7:15 (Paul has ‘you’; Cyril ‘us’). ‘End of law and prophets’: Romans 10:4 has ‘end of the law’ only; Cyril adds ‘and the prophets’, so the citation sits after ‘law’. LXX Psalm 118:96 = English Psalm 119:96. 2 Corinthians 6:11–14 quoted in full; ‘σπλάγχνα’ rendered ‘affections’. ‘ἡνωμένων ἐν πνεύματι’ could mean ‘in the Spirit’; kept lower-case ‘in spirit’ as the less committal reading. Cyril does not explain how 4 and 28 cubits yield ‘the eighth’; translated as it stands without supplying the arithmetic. ‘ἱστία’ (lit. ‘sails’, any woven sheet) rendered ‘cloth’. The Psalm 45:9 quotation (LXX 44:10) runs over into s.25; citation placed at the clause introducing it here and again at its close in s.25.

title: The colors and the pillars as figures of Christ
english: Cyril: …adorned in many colors’ (Psalm 45:9). Her adornment and beauty, in many forms, is Christ. He is one by nature, but he is understood through many different figures, for instance, as twisted linen. For the Word from God the Father, being fine and bodiless by nature, was in some way twisted through his interweaving, so to speak, with flesh. So he is twisted linen. He is also like blue, because he is not from the earth, but from above and from heaven; for the lofty, upper and ethereal body, which reaches even to the firmament itself, is in a way likened to blue. So he is like blue because he is from heaven, and purple because he is not a slave, as a creature is, but King from God and Lord of all. He is twisted scarlet: for, understood in his interweaving with flesh, as I said, and being truly the Word of God, he gave his own blood for us. Scarlet is a sign of blood. The figures of Cherubim on the coverings (Exodus 26:1) very well suggest, perhaps, that the things below have been joined to the things above, and that the Church on earth is now united to the powers in heaven. One should know that the most wise Solomon also carved Cherubim on the walls of the temple (1 Kings 6:29), and the design of the house shown through the voice of Ezekiel was made in this same way (Ezekiel 41:18–20). Over the curtains are coverings, fastened together with loops and rings (Exodus 26:7–11), and over these further coverings, blue skins and rams’ skins dyed red (Exodus 26:14). These hint at Christ, who shelters the Church: through the blue, again, as being from heaven and from above, and through the red color, as having come in flesh. For the color of flesh is something like that.
Palladius: I say this interpretation is not beyond reason.

Cyril: The curtains have pillars, a cubit and a half wide and ten cubits long, with their capitals and shafts covered all over with gold, and set on double bases of silver (Exodus 26:15–19; Exodus 26:29). Here again Christ is understood in each pillar: He is the support of the Church, the foundation of the truth, as Paul says (1 Timothy 3:15). He himself sets up and holds together all things. For through the cubit and a half it is indirectly suggested that he is perfect in the nature of Godhead, but lesser as one within the measures of humanity. It is not foolish to say that Christ is all-perfect, as in a whole cubit, since he is God by nature; but, as in half a cubit, lowered because of his humanity. For nothing among created things is perfect. Though he was rich, the Only-begotten became poor among us (2 Corinthians 8:9), and lowered himself into self-emptying (Philippians 2:7).
Palladius: True.
Cyril: So the humanity will not stand level with the surpassing heights of the Godhead; far from it. That is why he also said, as one who had become as we are and is understood as such:
translator_notes: Opens with the last word of the Psalm 45:9 quotation (LXX Psalm 44:10) begun in s.24. ‘ὑάκινθος’ rendered ‘blue’; Cyril compares it to the sky (‘the ethereal body that reaches to the firmament’). ‘συμπλοκή πρὸς σάρκα’ kept as ‘interweaving with flesh’ to preserve Cyril’s textile image (the first time softened by ‘so to speak’ for οἱονεί); not replaced with ‘union’. ‘ὡς γενητός’ rendered ‘as a creature is’. ‘ἄνωθεν καὶ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ’ may echo John 3:31; left uncited. ‘τῶν δειρέων ἡ γραφή’: Cyril places the Cherubim on the δέρρεις (coverings), though Exodus 26:1 has them on the linen curtains; translated as written, cited to Exodus 26:1. Solomon’s Cherubim: 1 Kings 6:29 (LXX 3 Kingdoms 6:29); Ezekiel’s temple: Ezekiel 41:18–20. Hair coverings with loops and rings (LXX κρίκοι, English ‘clasps’): Exodus 26:7–11; skins: Exodus 26:14 (LXX orders rams’ skins then blue skins). The LXX calls the tabernacle frames στῦλοι (‘pillars’; Hebrew ‘boards/frames’): Exodus 26:15–19 for size and the two silver bases, 26:29 for the gold overlay; Cyril’s ‘heads’ rendered ‘capitals’. ‘Support of the Church, foundation of the truth’ adapts 1 Timothy 3:15, where Paul calls the Church ‘pillar and foundation of the truth’; Cyril applies it to Christ. ‘He sets up and holds together all things’ may echo Colossians 1:17; left uncited. ‘ἐν ἡμῖν’ after ‘became poor’ rendered ‘among us’ (2 Corinthians 8:9 has ‘for your sakes’). Section ends mid-sentence; the quotation (John 14:28) follows at the start of s.26. ‘τὸ ἀνθρώπινον’ in the last turn rendered ‘the humanity’.

title: Gold and silver in the pillars; why the coverings are eleven
english: Cyril: …‘My Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28), although in the nature of Godhead he is equal in measure and falls short in nothing of the surpassing greatness of the One who begot him. The length of the post is ten cubits (Exodus 26:16). For Christ is all-perfect, as in the heights of the Godhead, and in the divine Scripture the number that reaches ten is taken as a sign of perfection. The post has a golden capital and a golden shaft as well (Exodus 26:29). Indeed, the temple born of the Virgin is made rich by the indwelling of the highest nature. Gold is a symbol of Godhead, since it ranks above all others, at least as far as such material goes. The base is of silver, and double (Exodus 26:19). Christ is bright and plain to see on earth, according to the saying: ‘God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us’ (Psalm 118:27). And the knowledge of him is, as it were, twofold, for in him are recognized both God and man. This, I think, is the meaning of the base being double, so to speak, and of silver.
Palladius: Your comparison is apt.
Cyril: But look at this, my good friend.
Palladius: What is it?

Cyril: He had commanded that the whole tent be spread out in ten curtains, and then he adds in between: ‘And you shall make coverings of hair as a shelter over the tent; you shall make eleven coverings. The length of one covering shall be thirty cubits, and the width of one covering four cubits; the eleven coverings shall have the same length. And you shall join five coverings together, and six coverings together, and you shall fold double the sixth covering at the front of the tent. And you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the one covering, the one in the middle at the joining, and you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the second covering that joins it’ (Exodus 26:7–10). What does this mean, then, Palladius? He sets up ten curtains. How, then, are the coverings not equal to them in number, but one is left over, that is, the eleventh? For he says: ‘You shall join five coverings together, and six coverings together’ (Exodus 26:9).
Palladius: I cannot say.
Cyril: But the arrangement will make clear what we are looking for.
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: He says that five curtains were to be fastened to one another, and another five, of the same form, set opposite in the same way. So when the two sets had been raised facing each other, from north and south, say, or from east and west, an eleventh side was then formed, running through the middle, with the ten on either side of it, divided into two sets. Over it, perhaps, the eleventh covering was stretched, holding both sides together with rings and loops. Its pillars were like those of the others, except fewer in number. For the ten curtains, as I said before, stretched to a length of twenty-eight cubits, while the eleventh, which lay in the very middle of the others, across the width of the five (and these are four cubits each),
translator_notes: Opens by completing the sentence begun at the end of s.25: Cyril quotes John 14:28 as ‘My Father is greater than me’ (John has ‘the Father’). ‘ἰσομέτρως ἔχων … οὐχ ἡττώμενος’ rendered ‘equal in measure … falls short in nothing’, keeping both negation and the reference to the Father who begot Him. ‘ξύλον’ (the LXX ‘pillar’ or frame of s.25) rendered ‘post’. Ten cubits: Exodus 26:16; gold overlay: Exodus 26:29; two silver bases: Exodus 26:19. ‘ὁ ἐκ Παρθένου ναός’ (Christ’s body as temple) has no single citation. ‘ὡς ἐν ὕλης τυχὸν τῆς τοιᾶσδε λόγῳ’ rendered ‘at least as far as such material goes’. LXX Psalm 117:27 (θεὸς κύριος καὶ ἐπέφανεν ἡμῖν) = English Psalm 118:27; the Hebrew-based English reads differently (‘The Lord is God, and He has given us light’). ‘διφυᾶ τὴν γνῶσιν ἔχει’ rendered ‘the knowledge of Him is twofold … God and man are recognised in Him’; Cyril does not use φύσις here, so ‘two natures’ was avoided. The LXX δέρρεις τρίχιναι (Hebrew ‘curtains of goats’ hair’) rendered ‘coverings of hair’. Exodus 26:7–10 quoted from the LXX; ‘the same length’ follows Cyril’s text (μῆκος). In the last turn Cyril’s reconstruction of the layout is speculative (‘perhaps’), and he uses ‘pillars’ loosely; kept as written. The section ends mid-sentence; the main verb (‘is stretched to about twenty cubits’) falls in s.27.

title: The eleventh covering and the court that widens
english: Cyril: …is stretched to a measure of about twenty cubits. That is why he says, ‘And you shall fold over the sixth covering at the front of the tent’ (Exodus 26:9), so that the part stretched out too far would not spoil the beauty of the court. In this one, then, set between the others as an eleventh, the holy and divine vessels were placed, which in themselves portray Emmanuel in many different ways. And perhaps the number also points to this: that in the last times of the age, at the eleventh hour, as it were (Matthew 20:6), Christ appears, and so does the tent that holds Christ, that is, the Church.
Palladius: There seems to be nothing unlikely in thinking that your account of this point is sound as well.

Cyril: After the words and types concerning the tent, he says: ‘And you shall make a court for the tent. On the side toward the southwest, hangings for the court of fine twisted linen, a hundred cubits long for the one side; and their pillars twenty, and their bases twenty, of bronze; and their rings and their bands of silver. So also on the side toward the east, hangings a hundred cubits long; and their pillars twenty, and their bases twenty, of bronze; and the rings and the bands of the pillars, and their bases, overlaid with silver. And the width of the court on the side toward the sea, hangings of fifty cubits; their pillars ten, and their bases ten’ (Exodus 27:9–12). Notice, then, that the first curtains were narrow, and their length ran to somewhere between twenty and thirty cubits, for they were four cubits wide and twenty-eight long. But those that came after them were broad and long indeed: a hundred cubits matched by a hundred, and fifty by fifty, one running toward the east, the other toward the west and the southwest.
Palladius: Then what does the riddle mean?

Cyril: Is it not plainly what was promised long ago through the voice of Isaiah to the Church revealed in the last times: ‘Enlarge the place of your tent and the coverings of your curtains. Fix them; do not hold back; spread out still further to the right and to the left’ (Isaiah 54:2–3)? For the Church of Christ, confined at the beginning, afterward widens to east and west, to north and south, and reaches every place.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: Notice too that all the other pillars, those of the ten curtains and of the one in the middle, he said must be overlaid with gold (Exodus 26:29) and set on double bases made of silver (Exodus 26:19). What this means has already been explained, I think. But the pillars of the long and broad curtains he adorns in a different way. He says they must be made richly splendid with silver from head to foot, and set in turn on bases of bronze overlaid with silver (Exodus 27:10–11, 17). This too would be a figure…
translator_notes: Bracketed editorial letters in the print ([ν] in εἰκοσάπηχυ[ν], διατετάν[ν]υσται) were read without the brackets. δέρρις = 'covering' (the goat-hair covering of Exodus 26:7), αὐλαία = 'curtain', αὐλή = 'court'. Cyril's arithmetic (an eleventh covering 'across the width of five' giving about twenty cubits) is his own reconstruction and is translated as given, not corrected. LXX geography: πρὸς λίβα (Exodus 27:9) kept as 'southwest' (λίψ, the southwest wind; Hebrew has 'south'); πρὸς ἀπηλιώτην (27:11) = 'east' (Hebrew has 'north'); κατὰ θάλασσαν (27:12) = 'toward the sea', that is, west. In 'στεναὶ μὲν αἱ πρῶται γεγόνασιν αὐλαί' the print has αὐλαί ('courts'), but the measures (4 by 28 cubits) are those of the tabernacle curtains (αὐλαῖαι, Exodus 26:2); rendered 'curtains'. 'εἰς τρίτην δεκάδα πήχεων' (into the third ten of cubits) = their length falls between twenty and thirty (twenty-eight). 'ἑκατὸν ἐφ' ἑκατόν, καὶ πεντήκοντα ἐπὶ πεντήκοντα' rendered 'a hundred matched by a hundred, and fifty by fifty' (two long sides, two short sides). Isaiah 54:2–3 LXX: Cyril joins ἔτι to μὴ φείσῃ; in the LXX ἔτι begins verse 3, so the English keeps 'still further' with 'spread out', which fits both readings; his text also reads 'τὰς δέρρεις τῶν αὐλαιῶν σου' (the coverings of your curtains). 'Eleventh hour' cited to Matthew 20:6 (the parable of the labourers; also 20:9). The gold pillars on double silver bases refer back to §26 and Exodus 26:19, 29, where the LXX calls the tabernacle boards στῦλοι; the court pillars of silver on silver-covered bronze bases follow Cyril's text of Exodus 27:11 (περιηργυρωμέναι) and 27:17. The last sentence breaks off: 'Τύπος' ends §27; 'δ' ἂν εἴη καὶ τοῦδε Χριστός' opens §28. The English splits it as 'This too would be a figure | of Christ.'

title: Silver pillars and the resonant gospel; oil for the lamp
english: Cyril: …of Christ. The silver shows that he shone out like light, flashing as God with rays the mind perceives. And the bronze overlaid with silver hints to us, indirectly, that the word he has spread over the earth, that is, the preaching of the gospel, is bright and resonant. For bronze rings clear, and silver is very bright and gleaming. This is true of the gospel preaching: one can see that the Savior’s word has the clearness and purity of the highest piety, and that it resounds, as it were, through the whole inhabited world. And if anyone prefers to see the holy apostles and evangelists figured in such pillars, his reasoning will be sound. For they are truly silvered, as it were, because they have come to share in Christ, who gives light. That is why it says, ‘And the brightness of the Lord our God shall be upon us’ (Psalm 90:17). They are also called ‘the light of the world’ (Matthew 5:14), and they all but stand on bronze overlaid with silver. For their support is, as it were, the bright and most resonant word they use. ‘For the Lord,’ it says, ‘will give a word to those who preach the good news with great power’ (Psalm 68:11). And it is written, ‘Beautiful too are the feet of those who bring good news of good things’ (Romans 10:15).
Palladius: The explanation is deep, but it comes close to the truth.

Cyril: Now that the commands about the court are complete, he turns to the preparation of oil, perfume and incense, saying: ‘And you, command the sons of Israel, and let them bring you pure oil from olives, free of dregs, beaten, to burn for light, so that a lamp may burn continually in the tent of witness, outside the veil that is over the covenant. And Aaron and his sons shall burn it from evening until morning before the Lord, a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations, from the sons of Israel’ (Exodus 27:20–21).
Palladius: And what does this mean?

Cyril: What it shows is most necessary, and I call the riddle a wise one. With the seven lamps (Exodus 25:37), which always burn and shine in the holy tent, we do well to compare the enlightenment that comes through Christ, which never fails in its power to shine into the mind of believers and to kindle it, or in other words to fill it. For the number seven in a way suggests completeness everywhere, as when it says, for instance, ‘The barren woman has borne seven’ (1 Samuel 2:5), that is, very many, as many as were needed to be enough. Aaron lights the lamps, and so do the rest, the priests who came after him. For the enlightenment from Christ is kept, as it were, unquenched in the churches through the uprightness of those to whom the priesthood has fallen, who make the minds of believers bright by their sound teaching of the mysteries. This, I think, is what is meant by lighting the lamps from evening until morning. And by darkness I take him to mean the deception that comes from the devil, a kind of night of the mind that comes over people, namely the…
translator_notes: Boundary: §28 opens with the rest of the sentence begun at the end of §27 ('Τύπος | δ' ἂν εἴη καὶ τοῦδε Χριστός'); English 'This too would be a figure | of Christ.' LXX renumbering: Psalm 89:17 LXX = Psalm 90:17 English ('καὶ ἔσται/ἔστω ἡ λαμπρότης κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν ἐφ' ἡμᾶς'; Cyril has ἔσται, the LXX ἔστω); Psalm 67:12 LXX = Psalm 68:11 English ('κύριος δώσει ῥῆμα τοῖς εὐαγγελιζομένοις δυνάμει πολλῇ'). 'Beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things' follows the wording of Romans 10:15 (τῶν εὐαγγελιζομένων τὰ ἀγαθά), itself from Isaiah 52:7; cited to Romans. 'Στεῖρα ἔτεκεν ἑπτά' = 1 Samuel 2:5 (1 Kingdoms 2:5 LXX). The seven lamps are not named in Exodus 27:20–21; cited to Exodus 25:37, where the seven lamps of the lampstand are commanded. Uncited possible allusions: the apostles as 'pillars' (Galatians 2:9) and the word resounding through the inhabited world (Psalm 19:4 / Romans 10:18); neither is clear enough to cite. 'ὁ περὶ γῆν αὐτῷ πεποίηται λόγος' rendered 'the word he has spread over the earth'. Exodus 27:20 LXX ἄτρυγον = 'free of dregs' (without lees). 'τὸ καταπέτασμα τὸ ἐπὶ τῆς διαθήκης' = 'the veil that is over the covenant', as in the LXX (the covenant meaning the ark). 'ἐπιείκειαι' (equity, decency) rendered 'uprightness'. 'ἐπὶ ταῖς αὐλαῖς' (about the courts) rendered 'about the court', since the court hangings are what precedes. The section ends mid-phrase ('τὰ τῶν | ἀνοσίων αἱρετικῶν ... μυθάρια'); the English ends '...namely the' and §29 continues 'unholy heretics' ...'.

title: Pure olive oil and true teaching; the lamps outside the veil
english: Cyril: …unholy heretics’ lightless and murky little fables. So the Savior’s light would be seen to be continual and unceasing in the churches, as long as the teachers in them rightly interpret the divine proclamations of the gospel. And the oil is pure; for the right and true teaching about the divine doctrines, unmixed with anything worse, is entirely free, as it were, of all dregs and dirt. It always stirs up the Savior’s light, not because it adds any brightness of its own to Christ (for it is utterly foolish to think that he needs a human being), but because Christ, being the true light (John 1:9) and the radiance of the Father (Hebrews 1:3), appears to the minds of believers as what he truly is through the sound words of the teachers.
Palladius: And why does he say the oil is to be from olives? Such exact wording is perhaps pregnant with some insight we need.

Cyril: You think very well, and I will tell you what comes to my mind. Those skilled in these matters, Palladius, are accustomed to make the oil we use not only from olives but also from various other seeds, spurious and earthier. The truly genuine oil will come from the finest olives; but the oil that comes, so to speak, from forcing and contrivance is somehow counterfeit and, as it were, not true, and by this I mean the oil from the earthier seeds. So we do well to compare the oil from olives with the word that is genuine and true, and that is supplied to the worthy through the wisdom from above (James 3:17). But the word devised from human notions and demonic inspiration is like the oil that comes from some people’s craft and peddling, and whose use is spurious. Such a word is useless and to be thrown away, and contributes nothing at all to the light of the knowledge of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). That is why it is not received in the churches. It does not have the fragrance of the Holy Spirit, for ‘no one says “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit’ (1 Corinthians 12:3); nor does it have the genuineness and unclouded clearness of the truth, which is needed if it is to do real good. Notice, too, that the law says the oil from olives must be brought by the sons of Israel (Exodus 27:20–21). For, as I said before, a true word will be our fruit and our spiritual offering to God, a word that does not let the light from Christ grow weak in those being initiated into the mysteries. The lamps are placed outside the veil, and they are lit there too (Exodus 27:21). For Christ, being light by nature, needs no light; but into us, who are outside the Godhead inasmuch as we are created, he puts his own light. For the ark lay within the veil (Exodus 26:33), as a figure and image of Christ.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: Then he says (Exodus 30:22–23): ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses: And you, take spices: flower of choice myrrh, five hundred shekels; and of fragrant cinnamon half of this, two hundred and fifty; and of fragrant…
translator_notes: Boundary: §29 opens mid-phrase ('ἀνοσίων αἱρετικῶν ἀφεγγῆ τε καὶ ἀμυδρὰ μυθάρια'), completing '...namely the' at the end of §28. 'φῶς τὸ ἀληθινόν' echoes John 1:9 and 'ἀπαύγασμα' Hebrews 1:3; both cited as clear verbal allusions. 'πρὸς φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως' is the wording of 2 Corinthians 4:6 (there 'of the glory of God in the face of Christ'); cited. 'σοφία ἄνωθεν' with 'δαιμονιώδης' and 'γεωδέστερα' echoes James 3:15–17 (wisdom 'from above' against wisdom 'earthly, unspiritual, demonic'); cited at 'wisdom from above' as James 3:17, with 3:15 behind 'demonic'. 1 Corinthians 12:3: Cyril has 'οὐδεὶς λέγει' (Paul: 'οὐδεὶς δύναται εἰπεῖν'); rendered as Cyril words it. Uncited possible allusion: 'καπηλεία' (peddling) may recall 2 Corinthians 2:17 ('peddlers of the word of God'); not cited. 'τόγε μὴν ... ἐξευρημένον, τὸ ἐκ τῆς τινων τέχνης' has no main verb; the comparison is carried over from 'παρεικαστέον', rendered 'is like'. 'ὠδίνει' (is in labour with) kept as 'may be bringing to birth'. 'γενητοῖς' = beings that came into existence (creatures); rendered 'created'. The oil 'from the sons of Israel' points back to Exodus 27:20–21 quoted in §28. Ark within the veil: Exodus 26:33. The new quotation is Exodus 30:22–23 LXX; the section ends mid-word ('καλά|μου', calamus), so the English ends 'and of fragrant' and §30 continues 'calamus'. The citation for the rest of the quotation stands at its close in §30. Review: the oil 'from the sons of Israel' cites Exodus 27:20–21, since 'παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ' closes 27:21.

title: The holy anointing oil: only God sanctifies
english: Cyril: …calamus, two hundred and fifty; and of iris, five hundred shekels by the shekel of the sanctuary; and there shall be oil from olives. And you shall make of it a holy anointing oil, a perfumed ointment made by the perfumer’s art. It shall be a holy anointing oil. And with it you shall anoint the tent of witness, and the ark of the tent of witness and all its vessels, and the lampstand and all its vessels, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offerings and all its vessels, and the table and all its vessels, and the laver and its base. And you shall sanctify them, and they shall be most holy. Whoever touches them shall be made holy. And you shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and sanctify them to serve me as priests. And you shall speak to the sons of Israel, saying: This shall be a holy anointing oil for you throughout your generations. Human flesh shall not be anointed with it, and you shall not make any like it for yourselves according to this composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you. Whoever makes any like it, and whoever gives any of it to a foreigner, shall be utterly destroyed from his people’ (Exodus 30:23–33). Now about the quality and the blending, and again about the unequal weights of the kinds named, I would have nothing to say; for truth is dear to those who are accustomed to think soundly. But oil blended with perfumes would signify, I think, the sanctification in Christ through the Spirit that is given to those who have received mercy, as in the words, ‘You anointed my head with oil’ (Psalm 23:5). The tent is anointed, and everything in it, for even a place may share in holiness through the one who dwells in it. The vessels too are sanctified, in the way that suits them, because they serve in the worship of God, and whoever touches them will be made holy (Exodus 30:29). So holy and sacred things may not be touched by those who are still profane; for, as it is written, ‘What fellowship has light with darkness?’ (2 Corinthians 6:14). And he absolutely forbids them to make a similar oil for themselves. For to sanctify belongs to God alone, and it will remain reserved to him as truly his own. How could a nature that has come into being and been made ever be able to sanctify others? For it is rich in holiness only with difficulty, through sharing in what comes from above. One might fittingly cry out to it in the words of the saints: ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ (1 Corinthians 4:7). For John also says of the Only-begotten, ‘From his fullness we have all received’ (John 1:16), and, ‘He does not give the Spirit by measure’ (John 3:34); rather, being himself the fountain of holiness, he imparts the Spirit to the worthy and sanctifies the rational creation. ‘But human flesh,’ he says, ‘shall not be anointed with it’ (Exodus 30:32), although he had commanded that Aaron and those who serve as priests with him be anointed with it (Exodus 30:30). So the sacred race is already above the human, since it shares in Christ, who is above creation. That is why, raising us to a dignity beyond nature, and cutting us off, as it were, from earthly things, he assigns us to the things above. For he says,
translator_notes: Boundary: §30 opens mid-word ('μου εὐώδους', completing καλά|μου from §29) inside the quotation of Exodus 30:22–33 LXX; the quotation's citation is placed at its close (Exodus 30:23–33), with 30:22–23 cited at its start in §29. LXX details: ἶρις (iris) is the LXX rendering of Hebrew 'cassia' (Exodus 30:24); kept as 'iris'. 'σίκλους τοῦ ἁγίου' = 'by the shekel of the sanctuary'. Where the LXX of 30:24 has 'ἔλαιον ἐξ ἐλαιῶν ιν' (a hin of olive oil), Cyril's text reads 'ἔσται' ('there shall be oil from olives'), possibly a misreading of ιν; translated as printed. 'Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων' (30:29) rendered 'most holy'. 'ἀλλογενεῖ' (30:33) = 'a foreigner'. LXX renumbering: Psalm 22:5 LXX = Psalm 23:5 English ('ἐλίπανας ἐν ἐλαίῳ τὴν κεφαλήν μου'). John 3:34 in John has God as giver; Cyril applies it to the Only-begotten as the source of holiness; translated as he uses it. 'ἐπιμετρεῖ' (measures out, bestows) rendered 'imparts', so that it does not seem to contradict 'not by measure'. 'τῆς τῶν ἁγίων φωνῆς' (the voice of the saints) introduces Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 4:7. 'πλουτεῖ μόλις ἐκ μετοχῆς τῆς ἄνωθεν' rendered 'it is barely rich in holiness itself, and only by sharing in what is from above'. 'τὸ γένος τὸ ἱερόν' (the sacred race, here the priestly people) may echo 1 Peter 2:9; not cited. Cyril admits he cannot explain the qualities, blend or weights of the spices; this is kept as an honest disclaimer, not smoothed away. Review: σκεύη rendered 'vessels' in the quotation, as in Cyril's comment and §27; ἁγιάσεις rendered 'sanctify' (not 'consecrate') so the quotation matches Cyril's argument that only God sanctifies.

title: Holy things kept from unbelievers; the incense no one may copy
english: Cyril: …‘call no one on earth your father; for you have one Father, who is in heaven, and you are all brothers’ (Matthew 23:9, 8). And the penalty for those who give any of the oil to a foreigner is destruction (Exodus 30:33). For he says, ‘Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine’ (Matthew 7:6). For to bring the hidden things, the things fit only for the holy, carelessly before those who are still unbelievers is full of danger. For what is sanctified is not what is still profane and grievously sick with uncleanness, but what has already been cleansed through holy baptism.
Palladius: True.

Cyril: In the same way and on the same principle he laid down how the incense was to be prepared, saying: ‘And you, take for yourself sweet spices, stacte and onycha, fragrant galbanum and clear frankincense, an equal weight of each, and they shall make of it a perfumed incense, the work of a perfumer, blended, pure, a holy work. And you shall beat some of it very fine and put it before the testimony in the tent of witness, where I will make myself known to you. The incense shall be most holy to you. You shall not make any for yourselves according to this composition; it shall be holy to you for the Lord. Whoever makes any like it, to smell it, shall perish from his people’ (Exodus 30:34–38). Here again the passage hints to us that the things specially reserved belong to the nature that is beyond all natures. None of the things that have been made has a share in them by essence, and creation has nothing whatever in common with its Maker and Master where rank and the preeminence of honors are concerned. We will recall, too, that we called both the golden altar and the compounded fine incense itself Christ, and said that Emmanuel himself is signified to us by both. Since, then, the incense points to Christ (for its fragrance is beyond compare), we will not make for ourselves incense like it. For we will accept no other at all besides him, as the wretched Jews indeed will: they will accept the son of lawlessness (John 5:43; 2 Thessalonians 2:3). For such people will be caught compounding for themselves an incense after the pattern of that fragrant and truly unique incense of God the Father, who has made manifest to us in the Son the fragrance of the knowledge of him (2 Corinthians 2:14). Through the Son we too give off a sweet fragrance (2 Corinthians 2:15), not because we have compounded the fine incense for ourselves, but because we share in the incense, have been anointed with the grace of the Spirit, and strive to win approval by the life we live in Christ.
Palladius: So it seems that through everything made in the holy tent the mystery of the Savior is given shape for us.
Cyril: And besides this you would be amazed to learn that even the craftsmen of the holy tent portray Christ, at least in their own persons.
Palladius: In what way do you mean? I cannot work it out.
Cyril: For it is written again: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe…’ (Exodus 31:1–2)
translator_notes: Section opens mid-quotation: the word «Πατέρα» and «γάρ, φησί» close §30; the English here supplies 'father' so the verse reads whole, so §30's English should end at 'For he says:' without the word 'father' (or the overlap be trimmed at merge). Matthew 23:9 is quoted with the clause 'you are all brothers' from 23:8 joined to it, cited as 'Matthew 23:9, 8'. 'Any of the oil' renders ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, which refers back to the anointing oil of Exodus 30:33 discussed in §30. Incense recipe follows Cyril's LXX text of Exodus 30:34-38 (ἴσον ἴσῳ = 'an equal weight of each'; ὅθεν γνωσθήσομαί σοι ἐκεῖθεν = 'where I will make myself known to you'; Ἅγιον τῶν ἁγίων rendered 'most holy'). 'Beyond all natures' renders ἐπέκεινα ἁπασῶν (feminine plural, taken with φύσεων). Μεμνησόμεθα (future perfect) rendered 'we remember'. ἐπ' αὐτῷ taken as 'besides him' (could also be 'after him'). The clause about the Jews has no verb of its own; παραδέξονται is understood from παραδεξόμεθα, and τὸν τῆς ἀνομίας υἱόν is its object; this is Cyril's polemic, kept as written. 'Son of lawlessness': the closest New Testament wording is 2 Thessalonians 2:3 (ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἀνομίας, with 'son of destruction'); the idea of receiving 'another' echoes John 5:43; both cited as allusions. LXX Psalm 88:23 (English 89:22) has υἱὸς ἀνομίας but in a different sense, not cited. 'The fragrance of the knowledge of himself' follows 2 Corinthians 2:14 (τὴν ὀσμὴν τῆς γνώσεως αὐτοῦ φανεροῦντι) with 2:15 (Χριστοῦ εὐωδία). Emmanuel used as a title (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23), not cited. 'Holy baptism' is Cyril's gloss, no citation. The section ends mid-word (φυ|λῆς) inside Exodus 31:2; §32 completes the quotation.

title: Bezalel of Judah stands for Christ, Eliab of Dan for the apostles
english: Cyril: …of Judah, and I have filled him with the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding and knowledge, to plan every kind of work in gold, silver and bronze, in blue and purple, in spun scarlet and twisted fine linen, and in stonework, and to work at carpentry in wood in every kind of work. And I myself have appointed both him and Eliab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, and to all who have understanding hearts I have given understanding, and they shall make everything that I have commanded’ (Exodus 31:3–6). Notice, then, how Bezalel directs the craftwork, while Eliab carries it out.
Palladius: And what of that?

Cyril: You will learn. Judah and Dan were both sons of Jacob, but one was born of Leah, a free woman, and the other of Bilhah, a maidservant (Genesis 29:35; 30:5–6). Bezalel, then, is a clear type of Christ, who appeared to us from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh (Hebrews 7:14), and from the nature that is truly free, that is, plainly, the divine and supreme nature. And Eliab would very well represent the apostles and evangelists who worked together with Christ, born as it were of Jerusalem the slave woman (Galatians 4:25). For they became God’s fellow workers (1 Corinthians 3:9), working with him as he, so to speak, labored and crafted all that served to establish the holy churches. And all who had understanding hearts contributed to the works of the tent whatever their own zeal and goodwill supplied, and so served as images of the teachers of every age, for whom it is a matter of zeal and care to do the work of God and whatever may serve the good of the Church of Christ.
translator_notes: Opens mid-word (φυ|λῆς) completing Exodus 31:2; the quotation runs through Exodus 31:3-6, cited once at its close. Cyril's text of 31:3-4 lacks the LXX's ἀρχιτεκτονῆσαι ἐργάζεσθαι, so διανοεῖσθαι governs the materials directly ('to devise ... the gold'); translated as it stands. ὑάκινθος rendered 'blue' (as in English Bibles). δέδωκα rendered 'appointed' (LXX ἔδωκα αὐτόν; Hebrew 'I have appointed with him'). Eliab son of Ahisamach is the LXX form of the name; English Bibles from the Hebrew call him Oholiab; Cyril's name is kept because his argument rests on him, and the reading page may add '(Oholiab)' if wanted. Leah as mother of Judah: Genesis 29:35; Bilhah as mother of Dan: Genesis 30:5-6 (Cyril spells her Βάλη). 'Free woman' and 'slave' follow Galatians 4:22-26; the explicit phrase 'Jerusalem the slave' matches Galatians 4:25, cited there only. 'From the tribe of Judah according to the flesh' cited to Hebrews 7:14 (ἐξ Ἰούδα ἀνατέταλκεν ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν); Romans 1:3 and Revelation 5:5 are near but not cited. 'God's fellow workers' = 1 Corinthians 3:9 (θεοῦ γάρ ἐσμεν συνεργοί). μονονουχὶ πονοῦντι καὶ τεχνωμένῳ: the dative refers to God as the master craftsman ('so to speak, labored and crafted'). The contributions of 'all who were wise of heart' take up the phrase of Exodus 31:6 already cited; the bringing of gifts recalls Exodus 35:10, 21-29, but Cyril quotes no verse there, so it is not cited. 'The fruits of their own zeal' renders the neuter τὰ ἐξ οἰκείας σπουδῆς (the things from their own zeal). The Greek text used here ends at ‘Church of Christ’ with no closing doxology, and none is supplied.
